Lead
Information for Renters
Updated 3/7/19
What is the Massachusetts Lead Law?
The Massachusetts Lead Law protects children from lead poisoning.
The Lead Law requires the removal or covering of any lead paint hazards in any home built
before 1978 where a child under the age of 6 lives. Lead paint hazards include loose lead
paint or lead paint on things like windows and door frames.
Homeowners and landlords are responsible for complying with the Lead Law. They are
required to make the home lead-safe if a child under 6 lives there.
Can a landlord refuse to rent to me or
evict me because of lead in the home?
No. According to MA laws and the Federal Fair Housing Act,
landlords CANNOT refuse to rent to you or evict you if you
have children or if the property has lead. Landlords are
responsible for correcting lead paint hazards in your home.
If you think a landlord has discriminated against you, call the
Boston Office of Fair Housing & Equity at 617-635-2500 or the
MA Commission Against Discrimination at 617-994-6000.
My landlord is doing work in my home. Is my family safe?
If you are unsure whether your landlord is doing work safely, call the Boston Childhood Lead
Poisoning Prevention Program (BCLPPP) at 617-534-5965.
BCLPPP inspectors can identify whether your home has lead paint. They can also tell you
whether work is being done safely and according to the MA Lead Law and the Deleading &

question: My landlord changed the locks while I was away for a week. Is this an illegal eviction in MA?
response:
Yes, changing the locks without a court order is considered an illegal eviction in Massachusetts. This is known as a "lockout," and it is illegal for a landlord to evict a tenant through self-help tactics such as changing the locks without a court's permission. If your landlord has done this, they may be violating both civil and criminal laws.

You can take the following steps:

1. **Write a Demand Letter**: Inform your landlord that they are committing an illegal act and that you will take legal action to enforce your rights if they do not rectify the situation.

2. **Go to Court**: You can seek a temporary restraining order (TRO) from the court. A TRO can order your landlord to stop the illegal action and restore you to your apartment, including changing the locks back and restoring any utilities if they were shut off.

You may also be entitled to money damages of at least three months' rent, plus any court costs and attorney's fees.

For more detailed guidance, you may want to consult with an attorney or contact legal aid resources such as MassLegalHelp.org or Greater Boston Legal Services.

[Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 12: Evictions (https://www.masslegalhelp.org/sites/default/files/2025-03/12%20Evictions%202025.pdf)]

When Is Eviction Illegal
In order to save money or get tenants out quickly, some landlords try to intimidate
tenants or force them out of their apartments without going to court first. Others try
to take shortcuts and hope that tenants do not know their rights. This section will tell
you some of the most common ways that landlords try to illegally evict tenants.
1. Lockouts and Utility Shut-offs
It is illegal for a landlord to take away your apartment through "self-help" tactics.
Your landlord has used self-help tactics and violated the law if they do any of the
following things without a court's permission:
 Moves your belongings out of your apartment;
 Changes your locks (which is called a "lockout");
 Shuts off your utilities (which is called a "utility shut-off"); or
 Substantially interferes in any other way with your use of the apartment.
If your landlord attempts to take away your apartment in any of these ways, they
may be violating both civil and criminal laws.5
a. What You Can Do
Write a Demand Letter
If your landlord threatens to lock you out or shut off any of your utilities, you may
be able to prevent the landlord from taking this illegal action by sending them a
demand letter. This letter informs them that they will be committing an illegal act
and that you will take legal action to enforce your rights if they break the law. See
the sample demand letter (Form 18). Save a copy of this letter so that if your
landlord does not act properly, you have proof that the landlord knew they were
violating the law.
Go to Court
If a landlord locks you out of your apartment or shuts off your utilities, you should
immediately go to court to get what is called a temporary restraining order, or
“TRO.” A TRO tells your landlord to stop doing something illegal and orders them
to put you and your belongings back into your apartment and restore any utilities
they may have shut off. A TRO is usually the quickest way to get your apartment
back. You may also be entitled to money damages of at least 3 months' rent, plus
any court costs and attorney's fees.6 For more about lawsuits for money damages
see Chapter 13: When to Take Your Landlord to Court - Breach of Quiet
Enjoyment. See a sample Temporary Restraining Order (Form 15).

question: What is the eviction process in Massachusetts? How long does it take?
response:
In Massachusetts, the eviction process involves several steps that a landlord must follow to legally evict a tenant. Here's a general overview of the process:

1. **Notice to Quit**: The landlord must provide the tenant with a written notice, called a Notice to Quit, which specifies when and why they want the tenant to move out. The notice period depends on the reason for eviction:
   - 7-Day Notice: For certain lease violations.
   - 14-Day Notice: For non-payment of rent.
   - 30-Day Notice: For no specific reason or other violations.
   - No Notice: If the landlord accuses the tenant of illegal activity.
   [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 12: Evictions (https://www.masslegalhelp.org/sites/default/files/2025-03/12%20Evictions%202025.pdf)]

2. **Summons and Complaint**: If the tenant does not move out by the date specified in the Notice to Quit, the landlord must have a constable or sheriff serve the tenant with a Summons and Complaint. This starts the legal process to obtain permission from the court to evict the tenant.
   [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 12: Evictions (https://www.masslegalhelp.org/sites/default/files/2025-03/12%20Evictions%202025.pdf)]

3. **Court Process**: The court will schedule a date for a First Tier Court Event, which is a mandatory mediation session. If the case is not resolved, it will proceed to trial. The court must notify the tenant of the trial date, and the tenant has the right to defend themselves, file counterclaims, and request a jury trial.
   [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 12: Evictions (https://www.masslegalhelp.org/sites/default/files/2025-03/12%20Evictions%202025.pdf)]

4. **Eviction Timeline**: The entire process can take several weeks to months, depending on various factors such as court schedules, whether the tenant contests the eviction, and if there are any delays in the legal proceedings. The court must schedule the First Tier Court Event at least 30 days after the filing of the Summons and Complaint.
   [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 12: Evictions (https://www.masslegalhelp.org/sites/default/files/2025-03/12%20Evictions%202025.pdf)]

For specific situations or further assistance, it is recommended to consult with an attorney or seek help from legal aid resources such as MassLegalHelp.org or Greater Boston Legal Services.

by Julia E. Devanthéry Italicized words are in the Glossary
The first and most important thing to know about eviction law in Massachusetts is
that a landlord cannot make a tenant move out of their home without going to court
first. No matter what a landlord or a landlord's lawyer says, a landlord must go
to court and obtain permission from a judge to evict a tenant.
If you get eviction papers and you want to stay in your apartment or you want more
time to find a new place, you must respond quickly to any documents you
receive and go to court to defend your case. Depending on your situation and
whether the landlord has followed the law, you may be able to prevent the eviction.
If you cannot prevent it, you still may be able to postpone it. In either case, if your
landlord has violated certain laws, you may be entitled to money to compensate you
for these violations.
If you do not defend yourself in an eviction case, chances are a judge will order you
to move out and you will have missed the opportunity to raise any legal claims or
negotiate an agreement about how to resolve the issues.
This chapter tells you how the eviction process works, what rights you have
throughout the process, how you can prevent an eviction, and how you might be
able to postpone an eviction while you find another place to live.
This chapter does not take the place of having a lawyer or provide you with every
detail involving evictions. But it will, along with forms at the end of the book, give
you enough information so that you can protect your rights.
When Can a Landlord Evict
In order to legally evict a tenant, a landlord must follow specific procedures. A
landlord must:
 Properly terminate a tenancy; and
 Get permission from a court to legally take possession of your apartment.
Evictions are not easy and can be expensive if a landlord fails to follow the law and
a tenant knows and enforces their rights.1 If you familiarize yourself with the steps
in the eviction process and are persistent, you may be able to stay in your apartment
longer or be awarded money for the landlord's violations of the law.

4. Tenants with Leases
If you have a lease, it will specify the reasons that your landlord can terminate your
tenancy and the steps they must take to do this (which must happen before the date
the lease is scheduled to end).
If your landlord tries to evict you before your lease has ended, most leases require
landlords to terminate your tenancy by first giving you a written Notice to Quit
before proceeding to court. Although many leases require 7 days' notice, the amount
of time is not set by law and may vary from lease to lease. Check your lease to see
how many days' notice is required before a landlord can take the next step in the
eviction process, which is to go to court.29
If your lease has an option to renew and you fail to renew it, your landlord does not
need to send you a Notice to Quit if they want you out at the end of your lease. In
this case, the day after your lease ends, your landlord can immediately serve and
then file papers in court and begin an eviction case without giving you a Notice to
Quit.
Check your lease to figure out whether it automatically renews itself or whether you
must renew it to prevent it from automatically ending. For more about how to figure
this out, see Chapter 4: What Kind of Tenancy Do You Have - How Long Is
Your Lease Valid.
If your landlord accepts your rent after your lease ends, you automatically become a
tenant at will and you are entitled to get a 30-day (or rental period) Notice to Quit
before a landlord files an eviction case in court.
5. Tenants without Leases
If you do not have a lease, you need to first figure out whether you are a tenant at
will or a tenant at sufferance (for more information see Chapter 4: What Kind of
Tenancy Do You Have).

treated like a contract between a park
owner and a tenant. While a park owner and tenant both have the right to end
their "contract" by ending the tenancy, a park owner does not have the right to
change your obligations under your agreement by increasing your rent unless you
agree to the increase.
In order to increase your rent, a park owner must end your tenancy and offer you
a new tenancy with a higher rent. The law permits the park owner to do this by
sending you a rent increase notice and a 30-day notice to terminate the tenancy at
the same time. If the tenant does not agree to the higher rent, the tenancy will end
when the 30-day period expires, and the park owner can then begin an eviction
proceeding. If the tenant wants to continue their tenancy, they can either pay the
rent increase or try to negotiate a lower increase.

2. Terminating the Tenancy
To end or terminate a tenancy, a park owner must give you a written eviction
notice.58 Mobile home laws tell the park owner how and when they can deliver
the notice, what the notice must say, and what you can do to protect yourself
after you have received a notice.
 The park owner must deliver a written "Notice of Termination" to the park
tenant by certified or registered mail.
 The notice must be mailed at least 30 days before the date the park owner
intends to end your tenancy.
 The notice must specify the reason or reasons for the termination in the
notice, including whether the eviction is based on non-payment of rent, or
whether it is based on a violation of a provision of your lease or a rule of
the park. If the park owner sends you an eviction notice based on a lease
or rule violation, the notice should tell you what lease provision or rule
you violated, when you violated it, and how you violated it.
 The notice must inform the park tenant that eviction can be avoided if the
tenant pays the overdue rent or "cures" or corrects lease or rule violations
within 15 days from the date of the mailing of the notice. If a park owner
fails to notify a park tenant about their right to cure, the notice may be
invalid and the park owner may not be permitted to bring an eviction case
against you.
If the purpose of the notice is to increase your rent, it should tell you the new
amount of the rent and the date the rent increase is to take effect.
3. Defending an Eviction in Court
Once the notice of termination expires, a park owner can file an eviction case in
court under a procedure called a summary process action.
Summary process cases against mobile home tenants proceed according to the
same rules as an eviction case in any other residential tenant-park owner
situation. Park tenants have defenses, counterclaims, and legal remedies, like
other tenants. For more see Chapter 12: Evictions.
In every summary process case, it is always a park owner's responsibility to
prove that the tenant committed the specific violation stated in the notice of
termination. If the park owner cannot prove that you did the things they claim,
you should not be evicted.
Park tenants can also defend themselves in an eviction case based on the special
rights they have under mobile home laws.

question: My landlord shut off my hot water to try to get me to move out. What can I do? (MA)
response:
In Massachusetts, landlords are required to provide essential services such as hot water. If your landlord has shut off your hot water, they are violating the Massachusetts Sanitary Code, which sets minimum requirements for housing, including the provision of hot water [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 8: Getting Repairs Made (https://www.masslegalhelp.org/sites/default/files/2025-03/08%20Getting%20Repairs%20Made%202025_0.pdf)].

Here are steps you can take:

1. **Notify Your Landlord**: Inform your landlord in writing about the issue and request that the hot water be restored immediately.

2. **Contact the Board of Health**: If your landlord does not restore the hot water, contact your local Board of Health to request an inspection. A housing inspector can examine your home to see if it follows the state Sanitary Code. If there are violations, an inspector can order your landlord to make repairs within a certain time [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 8: Getting Repairs Made (https://www.masslegalhelp.org/sites/default/files/2025-03/08%20Getting%20Repairs%20Made%202025_0.pdf)].

3. **Document the Problem**: Take photos or videos of the issue and keep records of all communications with your landlord.

4. **Legal Action**: You may consider taking legal action against your landlord. If you prove the landlord broke the law, a judge may order them to restore services or pay you money for bad conditions [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 8: Getting Repairs Made (https://www.masslegalhelp.org/sites/default/files/2025-03/08%20Getting%20Repairs%20Made%202025_0.pdf)].

5. **Withhold Rent**: You may have the right to withhold rent until the hot water is restored. However, you should put the withheld rent money in a separate bank account to protect yourself from eviction if your landlord takes you to court. It is advisable to consult with an attorney before withholding rent [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 8: Getting Repairs Made (https://www.masslegalhelp.org/sites/default/files/2025-03/08%20Getting%20Repairs%20Made%202025_0.pdf)].

For specific legal advice, it is recommended to consult with an attorney. You can also find more resources and assistance at MassLegalHelp.org or contact Greater Boston Legal Services.

The Massachusetts Lead Law protects children from lead poisoning.

question: Can my landlord make me pay for professional carpet cleaning when I move out in MA?
response:
In Massachusetts, a landlord cannot require a tenant to pay for professional carpet cleaning as a condition of returning a security deposit. According to Massachusetts law, a landlord can only use a security deposit to cover unpaid rent or to repair damages caused by the tenant or their guests beyond normal wear and tear. Routine cleaning, such as carpet cleaning, is generally considered normal wear and tear and should not be deducted from a security deposit.

If you left your apartment in the same condition as you found it, minus reasonable wear and tear, the landlord must return your security deposit balance, with interest, within 30 days after you move out. If the landlord does not return your security deposit, you can send them a demand letter or take legal action in small claims court.

For more detailed information, you can refer to Legal Tactics Chapter 3: Security Deposits [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 3: Security Deposits (https://www.masslegalhelp.org/sites/default/files/2025-10/03%20Security%20Deposits%202025-%20Updated%208-13-25.pdf)].

question: I reported code violations and now my landlord is trying to evict me. Is this retaliation? (MA)
response:
In Massachusetts, it is illegal for a landlord to evict you in retaliation for reporting code violations. According to Massachusetts law, a landlord cannot evict you, raise your rent, or make a major change in your rental agreement because you reported bad conditions in your apartment or building to the Board of Health or other local officials. This is considered retaliatory eviction, which is prohibited.

To protect yourself, it is important to document your communications with your landlord. Keep copies of any written notices or emails you sent regarding the code violations. If your landlord takes you to court, you will need proof that you reported the violations.

If a court finds that your landlord has retaliated against you, it can order them to pay you up to three months’ rent as damages.

For more detailed guidance, you may want to consult an attorney or reach out to local legal aid resources such as MassLegalHelp.org or Greater Boston Legal Services.

[Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 8: Getting Repairs Made (https://www.masslegalhelp.org/sites/default/files/2025-03/08%20Getting%20Repairs%20Made%202025_0.pdf)]

What is the Massachusetts Lead Law?
The Massachusetts Lead Law protects children from lead poisoning.
The Lead Law requires the removal or covering of any lead paint hazards in any home built
before 1978 where a child under the age of 6 lives. Lead paint hazards include loose lead
paint or lead paint on things like windows and door frames.
Homeowners and landlords are responsible for complying with the Lead Law. They are
required to make the home lead-safe if a child under 6 lives there.
Can a landlord refuse to rent to me or
evict me because of lead in the home?
No. According to MA laws and the Federal Fair Housing Act,
landlords CANNOT refuse to rent to you or evict you if you
have children or if the property has lead. Landlords are
responsible for correcting lead paint hazards in your home.
If you think a landlord has discriminated against you, call the
Boston Office of Fair Housing & Equity at 617-635-2500 or the
MA Commission Against Discrimination at 617-994-6000.
My landlord is doing work in my home. Is my family safe?
If you are unsure whether your landlord is doing work safely, call the Boston Childhood Lead
Poisoning Prevention Program (BCLPPP) at 617-534-5965.
BCLPPP inspectors can identify whether your home has lead paint. They can also tell you
whether work is being done safely and according to the MA Lead Law and the Deleading &
Lead Safe Renovation Regulations.
Is my home's water safe?
The water provided to your home by Massachusetts Water Resource Authority (MWRA) is
safe. They test it regularly.
The service line that connects your home to the MWRA's water may contain lead. Find out
whether your home's service line is made from lead by checking the Boston Water and Sewer
Commission’s (BWSC) lead service line map at www.bwsc.org or by calling 617-989-7888.

question: What is the Section 8 housing program and how do I apply in Boston?
response:
The Section 8 housing program, also known as the Housing Choice Voucher Program, is a federal assistance program that helps low-income families, the elderly, and the disabled afford housing in the private market. Participants receive vouchers that subsidize their rent, allowing them to pay a portion of their income towards rent while the voucher covers the remaining cost.

To apply for Section 8 in Boston, you would typically need to contact the local public housing agency (PHA) that administers the program. In Boston, this is often managed by the Boston Housing Authority (BHA). The application process can vary, but generally involves:

1. **Checking Eligibility**: Eligibility is based on factors such as income, family size, and citizenship status. You must meet the income limits set by the program.

2. **Submitting an Application**: Applications are usually submitted during open enrollment periods. You may need to provide documentation such as proof of income, identification, and information about your household.

3. **Waiting List**: Due to high demand, there is often a waiting list for Section 8 vouchers. The waiting time can vary significantly.

4. **Receiving a Voucher**: Once you receive a voucher, you can search for housing that meets the program's requirements. The housing must pass an inspection to ensure it meets health and safety standards.

For specific guidance and to start the application process, you should contact the Boston Housing Authority or visit their website. Additionally, for more information, you can visit resources like MassLegalHelp.org or Greater Boston Legal Services.

question: My landlord never gave me a statement of condition for my security deposit. Does this matter? (MA)
response:
Yes, it does matter. In Massachusetts, if a landlord takes a security deposit, they are required to provide a Statement of Condition within 10 days of the tenant moving in. This statement should list any existing damage in the apartment. If the landlord fails to provide this, you can create your own Statement of Condition and send it to the landlord, keeping a copy for yourself. This can help protect you if there are disputes about the condition of the apartment when you move out. 

For more information, you can refer to the Legal Tactics guide on security deposits: [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 3: Security Deposits (https://www.masslegalhelp.org/sites/default/files/2025-10/03%20Security%20Deposits%202025-%20Updated%208-13-25.pdf)].

What is the Massachusetts Lead Law?
The Massachusetts Lead Law protects children from lead poisoning.
The Lead Law requires the removal or covering of any lead paint hazards in any home built
before 1978 where a child under the age of 6 lives. Lead paint hazards include loose lead
paint or lead paint on things like windows and door frames.
Homeowners and landlords are responsible for complying with the Lead Law. They are
required to make the home lead-safe if a child under 6 lives there.
Can a landlord refuse to rent to me or
evict me because of lead in the home?
No. According to MA laws and the Federal Fair Housing Act,
landlords CANNOT refuse to rent to you or evict you if you
have children or if the property has lead. Landlords are
responsible for correcting lead paint hazards in your home.
If you think a landlord has discriminated against you, call the
Boston Office of Fair Housing & Equity at 617-635-2500 or the
MA Commission Against Discrimination at 617-994-6000.
My landlord is doing work in my home. Is my family safe?
If you are unsure whether your landlord is doing work safely, call the Boston Childhood Lead
Poisoning Prevention Program (BCLPPP) at 617-534-5965.
BCLPPP inspectors can identify whether your home has lead paint. They can also tell you
whether work is being done safely and according to the MA Lead Law and the Deleading &
Lead Safe Renovation Regulations.
Is my home's water safe?
The water provided to your home by Massachusetts Water Resource Authority (MWRA) is
safe. They test it regularly.
The service line that connects your home to the MWRA's water may contain lead. Find out
whether your home's service line is made from lead by checking the Boston Water and Sewer
Commission’s (BWSC) lead service line map at www.bwsc.org or by calling 617-989-7888.

question: Can my landlord charge me for bed bug treatment in Massachusetts?
response:
In Massachusetts, landlords are generally responsible for maintaining rental units in a habitable condition, which includes addressing pest infestations like bed bugs. According to the Massachusetts Sanitary Code, landlords must ensure that rental properties are free from pests and vermin. Therefore, landlords cannot typically charge tenants for bed bug treatment unless the tenant caused the infestation through their own negligence or actions.

For more detailed information, you can refer to the City of Boston's guidelines on bed bug prevention and extermination, which outline the responsibilities of landlords and tenants in dealing with bed bugs. If you have specific concerns or need assistance, it may be helpful to consult legal aid resources such as MassLegalHelp.org or contact Greater Boston Legal Services.

What is the Massachusetts Lead Law?
The Massachusetts Lead Law protects children from lead poisoning.
The Lead Law requires the removal or covering of any lead paint hazards in any home built
before 1978 where a child under the age of 6 lives. Lead paint hazards include loose lead
paint or lead paint on things like windows and door frames.
Homeowners and landlords are responsible for complying with the Lead Law. They are
required to make the home lead-safe if a child under 6 lives there.
Can a landlord refuse to rent to me or
evict me because of lead in the home?
No. According to MA laws and the Federal Fair Housing Act,
landlords CANNOT refuse to rent to you or evict you if you
have children or if the property has lead. Landlords are
responsible for correcting lead paint hazards in your home.
If you think a landlord has discriminated against you, call the
Boston Office of Fair Housing & Equity at 617-635-2500 or the
MA Commission Against Discrimination at 617-994-6000.
My landlord is doing work in my home. Is my family safe?
If you are unsure whether your landlord is doing work safely, call the Boston Childhood Lead
Poisoning Prevention Program (BCLPPP) at 617-534-5965.
BCLPPP inspectors can identify whether your home has lead paint. They can also tell you
whether work is being done safely and according to the MA Lead Law and the Deleading &
Lead Safe Renovation Regulations.
Is my home's water safe?
The water provided to your home by Massachusetts Water Resource Authority (MWRA) is
safe. They test it regularly.
The service line that connects your home to the MWRA's water may contain lead. Find out
whether your home's service line is made from lead by checking the Boston Water and Sewer
Commission’s (BWSC) lead service line map at www.bwsc.org or by calling 617-989-7888.

question: How do I request a reasonable accommodation for my disability from my landlord in Boston?
response:
To request a reasonable accommodation for your disability from your landlord in Boston, you should submit your request in writing. The request should specify the reason(s) you need an accommodation and what specific accommodation you are seeking. It's important to clearly outline how your disability relates to the accommodation you are requesting. 

While the sources provided do not specifically address requests to private landlords, the process for requesting reasonable accommodations generally involves similar steps as those outlined for public housing authorities like the Boston Housing Authority (BHA). For more detailed guidance tailored to your specific situation, consider consulting resources like MassLegalHelp.org or contacting Greater Boston Legal Services.

[Source: Grievances and Appeals (https://www.bostonhousing.org/en/FAQ.aspx)]

[[Grievances and Appeals] What if my disability relates to the action(s) taken against my application? (https://www.bostonhousing.org/en/FAQ.aspx)]
**Q: What if my disability relates to the action(s) taken against my application?**

If you have a disability that relates to the reason you were found ineligible for assistance or priority status or the reason your application was withdrawn, you have the right to request a Reasonable Accommodation. You must request a Reasonable Accommodation in writing, specifying the reason(s) you need an accommodation and what accommodation you are seeking. You may deliver this request to the Department of Grievances and Appeals at any time prior to your hearing. The BHA may contact you to request additional information.

---

[[Reasonable Accommodation] How is my Reasonable Accommodation request reviewed in the context of other requests? (https://www.bostonhousing.org/en/FAQ.aspx)]
**Q: How is my Reasonable Accommodation request reviewed in the context of other requests?**

The BHA considers each request for reasonable accommodation as a separate request. Just because one person had a change approved or denied in the past does not mean that all requests for that type of change will be approved or denied. The decision will be made on a case-by-case basis with the understanding that each person’s needs and circumstances are unique.

---

[[Grievances and Appeals] What if my disability would prevent me from coming to the hearing or fully participating in the hearing? (https://www.bostonhousing.org/en/FAQ.aspx)]
**Q: What if my disability would prevent me from coming to the hearing or fully participating in the hearing?**

If your disability would prevent or impede your ability to physically attend the hearing, or if your disability would prevent or impede your participation in the hearing, you have the right to request a Reasonable Accommodation. You must request a Reasonable Accommodation in writing, specifying the reason(s) you need an accommodation and what accommodation you are seeking. You may deliver this request to the Department of Grievances and Appeals at any time prior to your hearing. The BHA may contact you to request additional information.

question: My apartment doesn't have working smoke detectors. Is my landlord required to install them? (MA)
response:
Yes, your landlord is required to provide, install, and maintain operable smoke detectors in your residence. According to the Massachusetts State Sanitary Code, the owner must ensure that smoke detectors and carbon monoxide alarms are installed and maintained in every residence as required by law. If there is a violation of this requirement, the local board of health must notify the chief of the local fire department. [Source: 105 CMR 410 — Minimum Standards of Fitness for Human Habitation (https://www.mass.gov/doc/105-cmr-410-minimum-standards-of-fitness-for-human-habitation-state-sanitary-code-chapter-ii/download)].

For specific legal advice or assistance, you may want to consult an attorney or contact resources like MassLegalHelp.org or Greater Boston Legal Services.

[105 CMR 410 — Minimum Standards of Fitness for Human Habitation (State Sanitary Code Chapter II) (https://www.mass.gov/doc/105-cmr-410-minimum-standards-of-fitness-for-human-habitation-state-sanitary-code-chapter-ii/download)]
## 410.330: Smoke Detectors and Carbon Monoxide Alarms
(A) The owner shall provide, install, and maintain in operable condition smoke detectors and
carbon monoxide alarms in every residence that is required to be equipped with smoke detectors
and carbon monoxide alarms in accordance with M.G.L. c. 148, §§ 26 C-F½ and 780 CMR:
Massachusetts State Building Code, 527 CMR 1.00: Massachusetts Comprehensive Fire Safety
Code, and 248 CMR 10.00: Uniform State Plumbing Code and in compliance with accepted
standards.
(B) The board of health shall immediately notify the chief of the local fire department of any
violation of 105 CMR 410.330 which is observed during an inspection of any residence.
(C) If any residence is found by the local fire department to be adequately equipped with smoke
detectors and carbon monoxide alarms, the board of health shall not be authorized by 105 CMR
410.330 to impose any additional or differing smoke detector or carbon monoxide alarm
requirement beyond that which has been found sufficient by the local fire department.

question: Can my landlord keep my security deposit for normal wear and tear in Massachusetts?
response:
No, your landlord cannot keep your security deposit for normal wear and tear in Massachusetts. The security deposit can only be used for repairs for damage that are not considered "reasonable wear and tear," unpaid rent, or unpaid real estate tax increase if your contract requires it. Normal wear and tear, such as routine painting, cleaning, and small repairs, cannot be deducted from your security deposit. [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 3: Security Deposits (https://www.masslegalhelp.org/sites/default/files/2025-10/03%20Security%20Deposits%202025-%20Updated%208-13-25.pdf)].

For more specific situations, it is recommended to consult an attorney or visit resources like MassLegalHelp.org or Greater Boston Legal Services.

[Attorney General's Guide to Landlord and Tenant Rights (https://www.mass.gov/guides/the-attorney-generals-guide-to-landlord-and-tenant-rights)]
## Payments at the start of tenancy

A landlord may only ask a tenant for the following up-front payments:
- The first month's rent
- A security deposit to cover the cost of any damage to the apartment beyond normal wear and tear (which may not exceed the amount of one month's rent)
- The last month's rent
- The actual cost of a new lock and key for the apartment

Landlords may not charge tenants or prospective tenants up-front pet fees, broker fees, or application fees at the start of a tenancy.

### Security deposits
All security deposits must be deposited in a Massachusetts bank, in an account that collects interest, and within the first month of the tenancy. The deposit must be kept separate from the landlord's money in an account that is protected from the landlord's creditors. The landlord must provide the tenant with the name and address of the bank holding the security deposit, plus the actual account number. Each year, the landlord must either pay the tenant the interest on the security deposit or let the tenant deduct that amount from a rent payment.

The landlord should give the tenant a "statement of condition" within 10 days of beginning the tenancy or upon receipt of the security deposit (whichever is later), which describes the condition of the apartment and any damage that exists at that time. The tenant has 15 days to add to the "statement of condition" or make changes to it.

When the tenancy ends, the landlord must return the security deposit, plus interest, within 30 days. However, the landlord may keep any unpaid rent or the amount of money needed to repair damage done to the apartment beyond normal wear and tear.

### Last month's rent
If the tenant provides the landlord with the last month's rent at the commencement of the tenancy, then the landlord must give the tenant a signed receipt. At the end of each year and when the tenancy ends, the tenant is entitled to any interest earned on the last month's rent.

question: I'm a domestic violence survivor. Can I break my lease in Massachusetts?
response:
Yes, as a survivor of domestic violence in Massachusetts, you may have the right to break your lease early. Massachusetts law provides survivors with the right to break their lease without penalty. This protection is also supported under the federal Violence Against Women Act (VAWA), which prevents survivors of domestic violence from being denied housing or evicted from certain federally funded subsidized housing due to the violence they have experienced. 

For more information, you can refer to the resources provided by MassLegalHelp.org or consult with an attorney for specific guidance on your situation.

5. Discrimination Based on Sex
While it is not extremely common for landlords to refuse to rent to someone
explicitly because they are a man or a woman, discrimination based on sex
most commonly occurs based on three different issues:
§ Domestic violence

§ LGBTQ discrimination

a. Domestic Violence
Landlords or housing providers often take action against survivors of
domestic violence because they are or have experienced domestic violence.
For example, a landlord might seek to evict a tenant who has been a victim of
domestic violence because the landlord believes the tenant will allow their
abuser to come back again and again. Or, a landlord might refuse to rent to a
survivor of domestic violence believing if they have experienced domestic
violence in the past, it’s likely they will again. Assumptions like this are
often based in gender stereotypes, and as a result, may be illegal sex
discrimination.67
Additionally, if a landlord has a blanket policy of evicting everyone in a
household after the police are called, that policy can unfairly result in the
eviction of victims of domestic violence. And, because victims of domestic
violence are disproportionately women, these policies may be illegal sex
discrimination.68
Survivors of domestic violence also have other legal rights, under both state
and federal law. Massachusetts law, for example, provides survivors with the
right to change their locks, break their lease early, and not be denied new
housing because of their history of domestic violence.69
Under the federal Violence Against Women Act (VAWA), survivors of
domestic violence who live in, or are applying to live in, certain federally
funded subsidized housing cannot be denied admission, denied assistance,
terminated from participation, or evicted from those federal program if the
basis for the denial or eviction is because of the domestic violence.70
b. LGBTQ Discrimination
State and federal law also provide protections against discrimination in
housing because of someone’s sexual orientation or gender identity.
Massachusetts law has explicitly protected tenants against discrimination
based on sexual orientation since 1989 and based on gender identity since
2012.71
In 2020, the U.S. Supreme Court recognized in the context of employment
discrimination that discrimination “because of sex” includes discrimination
because of sexual orientation or gender identity.72 Following the Court’s
decision, the federal government issued guidance making clear that it
interprets the federal Fair Housing Act’s prohibition against sex
discrimination to prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation or

Protections for Survivors of Domestic
Violence
1. All Housing
In Massachusetts, a landlord cannot reject your application for housing if you
had to end your lease early or change your locks at a previous apartment because
of domestic violence. This applies to all landlords and all rental housing.41
In addition, under the federal Violence Against Women Act (VAWA), survivors
of domestic violence who are applying to live in certain federally funded
subsidized housing cannot be denied admission or assistance if the basis for the
denial is because of the domestic violence.42 See the section in this chapter called
Federal Housing Assistance.
If you feel you have been denied housing for this reason, you can file a
complaint in Housing Court, District Court or Boston Municipal court and ask a
judge to require the landlord to rent to you. Denial of housing for reasons related
to domestic violence might also be considered discrimination based on gender. If
you feel that you are being discriminated against because of your gender see
Chapter 7: Discrimination.
2. State Housing Assistance
If you are applying for state housing assistance, a housing agency or housing
provider cannot reject your application if you have to end your lease early or
change your locks at a previous apartment because you faced domestic violence.
If you feel you have been denied a state rental housing voucher for these reasons
you can immediately appeal the denial in a hearing under the rules of the specific
housing program. For more about these rules see Challenging the Denial of
Housing. You can also file a complaint in Housing Court, District Court or
Boston Municipal court and ask a judge to require the housing agency to give
you subsidy.
If you have applied to privately-owned multifamily subsidized housing provider,
you can file a complaint in Housing Court, District Court or Boston Municipal
court and ask a judge to require the housing provider to give you housing.
Denial of housing for reasons related to domestic violence might also be
considered discrimination based on gender. If you feel that you are being
discriminated against because of your gender see Chapter 7: Discrimination.

The key to leaving your apartment without problems is careful and thorough
preparation ahead of time. This chapter will tell you what steps you should take

Your Responsibilities When You Leave
1. If You Have a Lease
If you have a written lease and you want to move out permanently, there are two
questions you need to ask yourself:
 When is my lease supposed to end?
 When do I want to move out?
a. Moving at the End of Your Lease
For a written lease to be valid, it must include the date on which your tenancy is
to end. If it does not contain an end date, it is a written tenancy at will agreement
and you should read the next section in this chapter, called If You Do Not Have
a Lease.
If you have a valid lease and you plan to leave on the date that your lease ends,
look in the first 10 or 15 lines of the lease to see whether your lease
automatically extends itself. If it does, it will say something like:
. . . this lease will continue in full force and effect after the above term
from year to year until either the Lessor (landlord) or the Lessee (tenant)
on or before the first day of the month in any year, gives to the other
written notice of intention to terminate this lease.
If your lease automatically extends, you have what is called a "self-extending
lease," and you must give your landlord notice that you are leaving. Your notice
must be in writing, and you must deliver it to the landlord by a certain date.
Check your lease to see when and how you need to give the landlord this notice.

question: What happens to my lease if my landlord sells the building in Massachusetts?
response:
If your landlord sells the building in Massachusetts, the new landlord must honor the agreements in your current lease. This means they must accept your old rent amount until your lease ends, or until they give you proper notice. The new owner cannot raise your rent or change the terms of your lease until the lease period ends or unless they provide proper notice as required by law.

Lead
Information for Renters
Updated 3/7/19
What is the Massachusetts Lead Law?
The Massachusetts Lead Law protects children from lead poisoning.
The Lead Law requires the removal or covering of any lead paint hazards in any home built
before 1978 where a child under the age of 6 lives. Lead paint hazards include loose lead
paint or lead paint on things like windows and door frames.
Homeowners and landlords are responsible for complying with the Lead Law. They are
required to make the home lead-safe if a child under 6 lives there.
Can a landlord refuse to rent to me or
evict me because of lead in the home?
No. According to MA laws and the Federal Fair Housing Act,
landlords CANNOT refuse to rent to you or evict you if you
have children or if the property has lead. Landlords are
responsible for correcting lead paint hazards in your home.
If you think a landlord has discriminated against you, call the
Boston Office of Fair Housing & Equity at 617-635-2500 or the
MA Commission Against Discrimination at 617-994-6000.
My landlord is doing work in my home. Is my family safe?
If you are unsure whether your landlord is doing work safely, call the Boston Childhood Lead
Poisoning Prevention Program (BCLPPP) at 617-534-5965.
BCLPPP inspectors can identify whether your home has lead paint. They can also tell you
whether work is being done safely and according to the MA Lead Law and the Deleading &
Lead Safe Renovation Regulations.
Is my home's water safe?
The water provided to your home by Massachusetts Water Resource Authority (MWRA) is
safe. They test it regularly.
The service line that connects your home to the MWRA's water may contain lead. Find out
whether your home's service line is made from lead by checking the Boston Water and Sewer
Commission’s (BWSC) lead service line map at www.bwsc.org or by calling 617-989-7888.

7. Following the Law
Your landlord must follow the security deposit law. If they do not, they must
return your entire security deposit when you ask for it. The landlord has
failed to follow the law if they:
 Do not give you a complete receipt within 30 days of getting your

Getting Your Security Deposit Back
1. What Can My Security Deposit Be Used For
a. While you are in the apartment
While you are living in the apartment, you and your landlord may agree to
use your security deposit to pay for rent or to repair any damage you or a
guest may cause. Your landlord can only use a security deposit in this way if
you and the landlord both agree to it.31 If you both agree, put the agreement
in writing. Both of you should sign it. Keep a copy.
b. When you move out
When you move out, your landlord can use your security deposit to pay for:
 Repairs for damage that are not "reasonable wear and tear."
 Unpaid rent, unless you legally withheld rent for bad conditions. See
Chapter 8: Getting Repairs Made.
 Unpaid real estate tax increase, if your contract requires it.32 See
Chapter 5: Rent.
Your landlord cannot use your deposit for:
 Damage that was already there when you moved in.

question: Can my landlord prohibit me from having a pet in Massachusetts?
response:
Yes, in Massachusetts, landlords can generally prohibit tenants from having pets in their rental properties. However, there are exceptions for service animals and emotional support animals, which are protected under federal and state laws. If you have a service animal or an emotional support animal, landlords must make reasonable accommodations for you.

For more specific guidance or if you believe your rights are being violated, it is recommended to consult with an attorney or reach out to legal aid resources such as MassLegalHelp.org or Greater Boston Legal Services.

a. What Is an Unfair or Deceptive Act
An unfair or deceptive act can be any action that violates existing laws or
regulations that protect your health, safety, or welfare.38 This can include:
 Violations of the local building codes, housing codes, and state Sanitary
Code;
 Violations of the Attorney General’s consumer protection regulations;39
 Retaliation;
 Charging you for utilities without a written agreement.
 Unfair debt collection practices;
 Refusing to make repairs after the landlord has notice;
 Violating your right to quiet enjoyment;
 Breaching the warranty of habitability;

 Not obeying the security deposit law;
 Sending you documents that look like court papers, but are not;
 Refusing to accept court papers from you;
 Using illegal terms in your lease;
 Omitting from your lease the name, address, or phone number of the
landlord or manager for your building; or
 Failure to give you a copy of your lease within 30 days after you signed it.
Many of the other claims listed in this chapter are also violations of the
Consumer Protection Act.
Finally, the law prohibits any other conduct by the landlord that you can
convince a judge was unfair or deceptive.40 To make sure you claim all possible
violations of the Consumer Protection Act (Chapter 93A), it is best to state at the
end of your complaint: "All of my claims are also violations of Chapter 93A of
the Massachusetts General Laws. This entitles me to double or triple all actual
damages given to me."
b. How to recover damages under the Consumer Protection Law
To recover damages under the Consumer Protection Act, the law requires that
you first send your landlord a written demand letter at least 30 days before you
file a lawsuit.41 The purpose of a demand letter is to tell your landlord how they
have violated the law and what you want them to do. This letter must describe
the landlord's deceptive act, how it is injuring you, what you want done, and a
request for a reasonable settlement.42 See the sample demand letters (Forms 5, 6,
10, and 18). This letter is not required if your consumer protection claim is raised
as a counterclaim in an eviction case.43 You should also refer to the information
about demand letters on the Attorney General's website at: www.mass.gov, then
type in "demand letter" in the search box.
If the landlord does not respond to your letter in writing after 30 days, you can
sue them.44 If the landlord does respond to your letter, but you do not think the
offer is reasonable, you may still sue. But the court may not award damages
greater than what the landlord already offered.45 If the landlord's refusal to settle
was willful or in bad faith, you can collect as much as two or three times the
amount you are demanding, plus reasonable attorney's fees and court costs.46 To
bring a lawsuit under the Consumer Protection Act, you must sue the landlord
within 4 years of when the landlord's unfair or deceptive act occurred.47
If other tenants are also affected or injured by the landlord's unfair or deceptive
acts, you can bring a class action lawsuit against the landlord.48

question: My landlord is deducting my security deposit for things that were broken when I moved in. What can I do? (MA)
response:
In Massachusetts, your landlord is not allowed to deduct from your security deposit for damages that were already present when you moved in. Here are steps you can take:

1. **Document the Condition**: If you have evidence, such as photos or a Statement of Condition, that shows the damages were present when you moved in, gather this documentation. A Statement of Condition should have been provided by your landlord within 10 days of your move-in, or you could have created your own and sent it to your landlord.

2. **Demand Letter**: Send a letter to your landlord requesting the return of your security deposit. You can use a Security Deposit Demand Letter (Form 6) available through resources like MassLegalHelp.org. Include any evidence you have that the damages were pre-existing.

3. **Legal Action**: If your landlord does not return your security deposit, you may consider filing a claim in small claims court. If the landlord is found to have wrongfully withheld your deposit, they may be required to pay you up to three times the amount of the deposit.

For more detailed guidance, you can refer to Chapter 3 of Legal Tactics: Tenants' Rights in Massachusetts, or consult legal aid resources such as MassLegalHelp.org or Greater Boston Legal Services.

question: How do I file a complaint about housing code violations in Boston?
response:
To file a complaint about housing code violations in Boston, you can follow these steps:

1. **Tenant Petition for Enforcement of the State Sanitary Code**: If you want a judge to order your landlord to repair conditions that violate the state Sanitary Code, you can use the Tenant Petition for Enforcement of the State Sanitary Code (Form 14). This form is specifically designed for tenants to request court intervention for repairs. [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 14: Using the Court System (https://www.masslegalhelp.org/sites/default/files/2025-03/14%20Using%20the%20Court%20System%202025.pdf)]

2. **Filing a Civil Complaint**: You can file a civil complaint in Housing Court or District Court. Housing Courts are often more familiar with landlord-tenant disputes and may offer more support. When filing, you must pay a filing fee, which is $135 in Housing Court and $195 in District Court. If you cannot afford the fee, you can file an Affidavit of Indigency to request a waiver. [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 14: Using the Court System (https://www.masslegalhelp.org/sites/default/files/2025-03/14%20Using%20the%20Court%20System%202025.pdf)]

3. **Board of Health Involvement**: You or the Board of Health can bring a complaint if the landlord fails to comply with the Sanitary Code. The Board of Health can also file a criminal complaint for violations. [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 8: Getting Repairs Made (https://www.masslegalhelp.org/sites/default/files/2025-03/08%20Getting%20Repairs%20Made%202025_0.pdf)]

4. **Criminal Complaint**: If the state Sanitary Code has been violated, you can file a criminal complaint in housing or district court. There is no charge for filing a criminal complaint. The court will schedule a show-cause hearing to determine whether the complaint should be issued. [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 14: Using the Court System (https://www.masslegalhelp.org/sites/default/files/2025-03/14%20Using%20the%20Court%20System%202025.pdf)]

For more detailed guidance, you may want to consult legal aid resources such as MassLegalHelp.org or Greater Boston Legal Services.

you owe someone more money than they owe you.

There are two kinds of criminal cases that tenants can bring against landlords
who fail to repair Sanitary Code violations. The first is where the landlord fails
to comply with the Sanitary Code.72 You or the Board of Health may bring this
kind of complaint.73 Fines for violations of the state Sanitary Code can range
from $10 to $500 a day.74
The second type of case is where the landlord fails to provide heat, hot water, or
other utilities or interferes with your quiet enjoyment. Only tenants who are
affected by the landlord's illegal behavior can file this type of criminal
complaint. To bring this type of complaint, you do not need a Board of Health
inspection, although it is very helpful. In addition to fining your landlord, a judge
can also sentence a landlord to serve up to 6 months in jail for violation of the
law of quiet enjoyment.
▲ Chapter 8: Getting Repairs Made

Receivership
As part of the tenant petition or civil complaint, a tenant may ask the court to
appoint a receiver.
1. What is a Receiver?
A receiver is a person or organization appointed by a court to temporarily
manage a property in order to enforce the state Sanitary Code and respond to an
irresponsible or absentee landlord. Tenants can use receivership as a strategy to
accomplish needed repairs and prevent a building from deteriorating.
Tenants get a receiver by asking a court to appoint one.75 If a court appoints a
receiver, the receiver usually is empowered by a court to:
§ Make repairs and improve the conditions.
§ Manage the building.
§ Collect the rents.
§ Pay expenses, including taxes and insurance.
Additional duties of a receiver vary depending upon what tenants request and
what a judge eventually puts in a written receivership order.
2. How to Get the Court to Appoint a Receiver
a. Filing a Tenant Petition or Civil Complaint
If you decide that you want a receiver, you need to go to court. If there is a
housing court in your area, go there. Housing courts have more experience in
dealing with receiverships than other courts do. However, you can also go to the
local district or superior court.76 For more about different courts see the Chapter
14: Using the Court System - Massachusetts Court System.
When you go to court, it is best to bring as many other tenants from your
building as possible. You can complete the Tenant Petition for Enforcement of
the State Sanitary Code (Form 14)77 or your attorney can draft a complaint for
you which could include claims for money damages due to bad conditions.
In the petition or complaint, you must specifically request the court to appoint a
receiver. You must also describe the bad conditions. Attach copies of the Board
of Health reports or, if an inspection has not been made yet, the date you
requested an inspection. It is best to get an inspection before you file a petition or
complaint.78

e. Contempt
When a landlord fails to follow the terms of a court order, they may be held
in contempt and punished by the court.35 For example, a landlord who fails to
make court-ordered repairs may be ordered to live in their building until the
repairs are completed.36
Criminal Cases
Criminal cases are pursued by the district attorney's office on behalf of the
citizens of the Commonwealth. They are violations of the law that carry
criminal penalties.37
Any person can file a criminal complaint with the court or ask the police or
health department to file a complaint on their behalf.
If the state Sanitary Code has been violated, the Board of Health can also file
a criminal complaint. For more about criminal complaints and Sanitary Code
violations, see Chapter 8: Getting Repairs Made. For a list of criminal
Chapter 14: Using the Court System ▲ 477

laws most frequently violated by landlords, see Chapter 13: When to Take
Your Landlord to Court.
Before you file a criminal complaint, ask yourself what outcome you want.
In many cases, a criminal complaint may take much longer time to get
results. For example, although you can file a criminal complaint if your
landlord won’t make Sanitary Code repairs, a civil complaint will move
through the system much faster, allowing a civil judge to issue repair orders
in just a few weeks. In comparison, a criminal complaint could take several
months to get a similar result.
1. Filing a Criminal Complaint
To file a criminal complaint, go to a housing or district court and ask the
court staff for a criminal complaint.38 Fill it out and return it to the clerk.
There is no charge to file a criminal complaint. You can also ask a Board of
Health or the police to file a criminal complaint on your behalf.
If you are in an area with a housing court, the housing court has criminal
complaints online. Go to:
www.mass.gov/info-details/criminal-proceedings-in-the-housing-court
The clerk will then schedule a hearing called a show-cause hearing to
determine whether your complaint should be issued by the court. The clerk
will schedule a show-cause hearing for the next available court date.
If it is an emergency and your physical safety is in immediate danger, ask the
clerk to schedule a show-cause hearing that day. You can also call the police
and ask that a criminal complaint be filed against your landlord.
2. The Show-Cause Hearing
A show-cause hearing is used by a clerk or magistrate to determine whether
your complaint should be officially issued by the court. It is less formal than
a court hearing.
At a show-cause hearing, the clerk will ask you to state the facts in your
complaint. A landlord may not have to be present at the show-cause hearing.
If the landlord is present, the clerk will then ask the landlord for their version
of events. The clerk must then decide whether the facts taken at face value
match what are known as the "legal elements" of a crime. The clerk does not
decide who is telling the truth or the guilt or innocence of your landlord. If
the clerk finds that the law may have been violated, they should issue a
criminal complaint.

Lead
Information for Renters
Updated 3/7/19
What is the Massachusetts Lead Law?
The Massachusetts Lead Law protects children from lead poisoning.
The Lead Law requires the removal or covering of any lead paint hazards in any home built
before 1978 where a child under the age of 6 lives. Lead paint hazards include loose lead
paint or lead paint on things like windows and door frames.
Homeowners and landlords are responsible for complying with the Lead Law. They are
required to make the home lead-safe if a child under 6 lives there.
Can a landlord refuse to rent to me or
evict me because of lead in the home?
No. According to MA laws and the Federal Fair Housing Act,
landlords CANNOT refuse to rent to you or evict you if you
have children or if the property has lead. Landlords are
responsible for correcting lead paint hazards in your home.
If you think a landlord has discriminated against you, call the
Boston Office of Fair Housing & Equity at 617-635-2500 or the
MA Commission Against Discrimination at 617-994-6000.
My landlord is doing work in my home. Is my family safe?
If you are unsure whether your landlord is doing work safely, call the Boston Childhood Lead
Poisoning Prevention Program (BCLPPP) at 617-534-5965.
BCLPPP inspectors can identify whether your home has lead paint. They can also tell you
whether work is being done safely and according to the MA Lead Law and the Deleading &
Lead Safe Renovation Regulations.
Is my home's water safe?
The water provided to your home by Massachusetts Water Resource Authority (MWRA) is
safe. They test it regularly.
The service line that connects your home to the MWRA's water may contain lead. Find out
whether your home's service line is made from lead by checking the Boston Water and Sewer
Commission’s (BWSC) lead service line map at www.bwsc.org or by calling 617-989-7888.

question: Can I sue my landlord in small claims court for not returning my security deposit in MA?
response:
Yes, you can sue your landlord in small claims court in Massachusetts if they fail to return your security deposit. According to Massachusetts law, a landlord must return your security deposit, with interest, within 30 days after you move out or the last day of your lease. If they fail to do so, you can take legal action.

You can sue for up to three times the amount of the deposit, plus interest and court fees. If you hire a lawyer, the landlord may also be required to pay your lawyer’s fees. The court must award triple damages if the landlord has failed to properly deposit the security deposit in a separate bank account, transfer it to a new owner, or return the deposit within the required timeframe. 

Most security deposit cases can be filed as a Small Claims case in Housing Courts, District Courts, and the Boston Municipal Court. [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 3: Security Deposits (https://www.masslegalhelp.org/sites/default/files/2025-10/03%20Security%20Deposits%202025-%20Updated%208-13-25.pdf)].

For more specific guidance, consider consulting an attorney or visiting resources like MassLegalHelp.org or Greater Boston Legal Services.

b. Taking Your Landlord to Court
You can take your landlord to court if they:
 Fail to respond to your demand letter;
 Fail to return your security deposit, with interest, within 30 days of the
day you move out, or 30 days of the last day of your lease;
70 ▲Chapter 3: Security Deposits

 Fail to give you a complete list of damages within 30 days after you
move out;
 Failed to give you a complete receipt within 30 days of your giving the
landlord a security deposit when you first moved in.
 Failed to put the money in a separate bank account that is protected
from creditors;
 Failed to transfer a security deposit to a new owner; or
 Asked you to give up your rights orally or in writing.
You can sue for up to $7,000 in Small Claims court. If your security deposit
was less than $7,000, you can sue for 3 times the deposit, even though 3
times that amount may be more than $7,000.
You can also sue the landlord for any interest they did not pay you during
your tenancy and for the amount of money you have to pay an attorney to
represent you.42
If you sue your landlord for your security deposit and they did not give you a
complete list of damages within 30 days of your tenancy ending, they cannot
claim you caused damage to the apartment. If the landlord wants to sue you
for damage to the apartment, they must start a separate case.43
The landlord is not allowed to keep any part of your deposit unless they send
you the list of damage and repairs within 30 days of the day you move out.44
c. Triple Damages

court finds that your landlord has failed to:
 Properly deposit a security deposit in a bank account separate from the
landlord's funds and protected from creditors;45
 Transfer a security deposit to a new owner; or

question: I just moved into a new apartment in Boston and my landlord didn't put my security deposit into a separate account. Is that allowed?
response:
No, that is not allowed. In Massachusetts, your landlord is required to keep your security deposit in a separate bank account in Massachusetts. The account must be separate from the landlord’s own money, and it must be clear that the money does not belong to the landlord. If a landlord fails to do this, you have the right to sue your landlord for three times the amount of your deposit. [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 3: Security Deposits (https://www.masslegalhelp.org/sites/default/files/2025-10/03%20Security%20Deposits%202025-%20Updated%208-13-25.pdf)]

For specific legal advice, it is recommended to consult with an attorney. You can also find more information and resources at MassLegalHelp.org or Greater Boston Legal Services.

A security deposit and last month's rent are not the same.
A security deposit is money you pay a landlord to protect them in case you

question: My landlord stopped paying the electric bill, and I'm worried about losing service. What can I do according to Massachusetts law?
response:
If your landlord is responsible for paying the utilities and fails to do so, the utility company must provide you with at least 30 days' notice before shutting off your service. During this time, you can take steps to protect your rights. 

You should contact the utility company to inform them of the situation and ask for protection from service termination. If the utility company does not assist, you can file a complaint with the Department of Public Utilities (DPU) by calling 1-877-886-5066 or filling out their online complaint form at mass.gov.

Additionally, if your service is at risk of being shut off, you may have special protections if your household is low-income, experiencing financial hardship, or if there are vulnerable individuals in your home, such as infants or elderly residents. 

For more detailed guidance, consider reaching out to legal aid resources such as MassLegalHelp.org or Greater Boston Legal Services.

[Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 6: Utilities (https://www.masslegalhelp.org/sites/default/files/2025-02/06%20Utilities%202025_0.pdf)]

question: Can my landlord charge me a pet fee in addition to my rent in Boston?
response:
No, in Massachusetts, it is against the law for a landlord to charge tenants any additional "moving in" fees, including pet fees. Landlords can only charge for the first month's rent, last month's rent, a security deposit, and the cost of a new lock and key. [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 3: Security Deposits (https://www.masslegalhelp.org/sites/default/files/2025-10/03%20Security%20Deposits%202025-%20Updated%208-13-25.pdf)].

What is the Massachusetts Lead Law?
The Massachusetts Lead Law protects children from lead poisoning.
The Lead Law requires the removal or covering of any lead paint hazards in any home built
before 1978 where a child under the age of 6 lives. Lead paint hazards include loose lead
paint or lead paint on things like windows and door frames.
Homeowners and landlords are responsible for complying with the Lead Law. They are
required to make the home lead-safe if a child under 6 lives there.
Can a landlord refuse to rent to me or
evict me because of lead in the home?
No. According to MA laws and the Federal Fair Housing Act,
landlords CANNOT refuse to rent to you or evict you if you
have children or if the property has lead. Landlords are
responsible for correcting lead paint hazards in your home.
If you think a landlord has discriminated against you, call the
Boston Office of Fair Housing & Equity at 617-635-2500 or the
MA Commission Against Discrimination at 617-994-6000.
My landlord is doing work in my home. Is my family safe?
If you are unsure whether your landlord is doing work safely, call the Boston Childhood Lead
Poisoning Prevention Program (BCLPPP) at 617-534-5965.
BCLPPP inspectors can identify whether your home has lead paint. They can also tell you
whether work is being done safely and according to the MA Lead Law and the Deleading &
Lead Safe Renovation Regulations.
Is my home's water safe?
The water provided to your home by Massachusetts Water Resource Authority (MWRA) is
safe. They test it regularly.
The service line that connects your home to the MWRA's water may contain lead. Find out
whether your home's service line is made from lead by checking the Boston Water and Sewer
Commission’s (BWSC) lead service line map at www.bwsc.org or by calling 617-989-7888.

1. Security Deposit
A security deposit and last month's rent are not the same.
A security deposit is money you pay a landlord to protect them in case you
damage the apartment. But a security deposit is your money. If you do not
damage the property and don’t owe any rent when you vacate, you generally
are entitled to get your full deposit back within 30 days after you leave.
(There are a couple exceptions, see When Can I Get My Security Deposit
Back - When your tenancy ends.
Your landlord must keep your security deposit in a bank account in
Massachusetts. The account must be separate from the account they keep
their own money in. And every year they must pay you the interest it earns.
2. Last Month's Rent
Last month's rent protects your landlord in advance if you leave and do not
pay rent the last month you are there.
Your landlord does not have to keep your last month's rent money in a
separate bank account. But they do have to pay you interest on it every year.
If you pay last month's rent in advance, do not expect to get this money back
when you move out. It will pay for your last month.
If you do not pay last month’s rent in advance, you must pay for your last
month of rent even if a landlord holds a security deposit.

fees, like:

**Q: What if my disability would prevent me from coming to the hearing or fully participating in the hearing?**

If your disability would prevent or impede your ability to physically attend the hearing, or if your disability would prevent or impede your participation in the hearing, you have the right to request a Reasonable Accommodation. You must request a Reasonable Accommodation in writing, specifying the reason(s) you need an accommodation and what accommodation you are seeking. You may deliver this request to the Department of Grievances and Appeals at any time prior to your hearing. The BHA may contact you to request additional information.

question: I'm renting an apartment in Boston and my lease is for 12 months. What are my rights regarding the security deposit my landlord is holding?
response:
In Massachusetts, your rights regarding the security deposit are governed by specific laws. Here are the key points:

1. **Amount**: Your landlord can charge a security deposit up to one month's rent. [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 3: Security Deposits (https://www.masslegalhelp.org/sites/default/files/2025-10/03%20Security%20Deposits%202025-%20Updated%208-13-25.pdf)]

2. **Use of Deposit**: The security deposit can only be used for unpaid rent, repairs for damages beyond "reasonable wear and tear," and any unpaid real estate tax increase if your contract requires it. It cannot be used for routine cleaning or repairs for damage that was already present when you moved in. [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 3: Security Deposits (https://www.masslegalhelp.org/sites/default/files/2025-10/03%20Security%20Deposits%202025-%20Updated%208-13-25.pdf)]

3. **Return of Deposit**: Your landlord must return your security deposit, with interest, within 30 days after you move out or the lease ends, whichever is later. [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 3: Security Deposits (https://www.masslegalhelp.org/sites/default/files/2025-10/03%20Security%20Deposits%202025-%20Updated%208-13-25.pdf)]

4. **Receipts and Statements**: Your landlord must provide a receipt for the security deposit and a Statement of Condition within 10 days of you moving in. If they fail to do so, you can create your own statement and send it to them. [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 3: Security Deposits (https://www.masslegalhelp.org/sites/default/files/2025-10/03%20Security%20Deposits%202025-%20Updated%208-13-25.pdf)]

5. **Separate Bank Account**: The security deposit must be kept in a separate, interest-bearing account in a Massachusetts bank. [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 3: Security Deposits (https://www.masslegalhelp.org/sites/default/files/2025-10/03%20Security%20Deposits%202025-%20Updated%208-13-25.pdf)]

If your landlord does not comply with these requirements, they may be required to return the entire security deposit to you. For more detailed information or assistance, you may want to consult resources like MassLegalHelp.org or contact Greater Boston Legal Services.

question: I just found out my landlord is selling the building. What happens to my security deposit?
response:
If your landlord sells the building, you should not lose your security deposit. The current landlord is responsible for transferring your security deposit to the new owner. The new landlord then has 45 days to notify you about the status of your security deposit, last month's rent, and any interest. If the new landlord does not send you this notice by the deadline, the old landlord must return your deposit plus interest. 

For more detailed information, you can refer to the relevant section in the Massachusetts tenant law resources: [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 3: Security Deposits (https://www.masslegalhelp.org/sites/default/files/2025-10/03%20Security%20Deposits%202025-%20Updated%208-13-25.pdf)]. 

If you encounter issues, consider seeking assistance from legal aid resources such as MassLegalHelp.org or Greater Boston Legal Services.

question: Can my landlord in Boston legally require me to pay for the cost of repairing normal wear and tear when I move out?
response:
No, your landlord in Boston cannot legally require you to pay for the cost of repairing normal wear and tear when you move out. According to Massachusetts law, a landlord cannot use your security deposit for damage that is considered "reasonable wear and tear." This includes routine painting, cleaning, and small repairs that occur as a result of normal use of the apartment. [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 3: Security Deposits (https://www.masslegalhelp.org/sites/default/files/2025-10/03%20Security%20Deposits%202025-%20Updated%208-13-25.pdf)].

Additionally, the lease must not include terms requiring the tenant to pay for ordinary wear and tear repairs. [Source: Attorney General's Guide to Landlord and Tenant Rights (https://www.mass.gov/guides/the-attorney-generals-guide-to-landlord-and-tenant-rights)]. If your landlord attempts to charge you for such repairs, you may want to consult an attorney or seek assistance from resources like MassLegalHelp.org or Greater Boston Legal Services.

the landlord and the tenant
Whether a tenancy is created by a lease or a tenancy-at-will, the tenant must pay rent, follow the rules agreed upon with the landlord, and accept responsibility for any damage to the apartment that is more than just "normal wear and tear". The landlord must provide an apartment that is safe, well-maintained, and in compliance with the Massachusetts Sanitary Code, and they must live up to any promises in the lease or rental agreement. The tenant has a right to occupy the apartment and the landlord may only enter under certain circumstances. The landlord must arrange with the tenant in advance to enter the apartment to make repairs, to inspect the condition of the apartment, or to show the apartment to prospective tenants, buyers or real estate agents. However, the landlord may enter an apartment without a tenant's approval if there is a mechanical/repair emergency that has the potential to damage the whole building, or if it appears that the tenant has abandoned the apartment.

## Terms of a rental agreement

Every rental agreement must have certain terms and is prohibited by law from containing certain other terms. The lease must set forth the name, address, and phone number of the owner, the person responsible for maintenance, and the person to whom the tenant can give copies of formal notices, complaints, or court papers.

The lease must not include illegal terms such as:
- Requiring the tenant to pay the cost of repairing ordinary wear and tear to the apartment
- Requiring the tenant to have the apartment professionally cleaned at the end of the lease
- Requiring the tenant to pay for repairs to parts of the building beyond the tenant's apartment
- Prohibiting the tenant from suing the landlord or reporting violations of the Sanitary Code
- Prohibiting the tenant from joining a tenants' union
- Requiring the tenant to pay a late fee if a rent payment is less than 30 days late

## Key rules for security deposits

### What landlords can collect at start of tenancy
A landlord may only ask a tenant for: first month's rent, last month's rent, a security deposit (max one month's rent), and cost of a new lock and key.

### Holding requirements
- Must be deposited in a Massachusetts bank in an interest-bearing account
- Must be kept separate from landlord's money
- Landlord must provide tenant with bank name, address, and account number within 30 days
- Failure to comply entitles tenant to immediate return of deposit

### Statement of condition
- Must be provided within 10 days of tenancy start or receipt of deposit
- Must list all existing damage
- Tenant has 15 days to add or modify the statement

### Interest on security deposit
- Landlord must pay 5% annual interest or the actual bank interest (whichever is less)
- Interest must be paid annually or tenant may deduct from rent
- If not paid within 30 days of year end, tenant may deduct from next rent payment

### Return of security deposit
- Must be returned within 30 days after tenancy ends
- Landlord may deduct: unpaid rent, unpaid water charges, tax escalation amounts, reasonable repair costs for tenant-caused damage (not normal wear and tear)
- If deducting for damages: must provide itemized list sworn under penalty of perjury with repair estimates/receipts

### Triple damages
- Tenant entitled to 3x the deposit amount plus interest, court costs, and attorney's fees if landlord:
  - Fails to deposit in proper bank account
  - Fails to transfer deposit to successor
  - Fails to return deposit within 30 days
