Lead
Information for Renters
Updated 3/7/19
What is the Massachusetts Lead Law?
The Massachusetts Lead Law protects children from lead poisoning.
The Lead Law requires the removal or covering of any lead paint hazards in any home built
before 1978 where a child under the age of 6 lives. Lead paint hazards include loose lead
paint or lead paint on things like windows and door frames.
Homeowners and landlords are responsible for complying with the Lead Law. They are
required to make the home lead-safe if a child under 6 lives there.
Can a landlord refuse to rent to me or
evict me because of lead in the home?
No. According to MA laws and the Federal Fair Housing Act,
landlords CANNOT refuse to rent to you or evict you if you
have children or if the property has lead. Landlords are
responsible for correcting lead paint hazards in your home.
If you think a landlord has discriminated against you, call the
Boston Office of Fair Housing & Equity at 617-635-2500 or the
MA Commission Against Discrimination at 617-994-6000.
My landlord is doing work in my home. Is my family safe?
If you are unsure whether your landlord is doing work safely, call the Boston Childhood Lead
Poisoning Prevention Program (BCLPPP) at 617-534-5965.
BCLPPP inspectors can identify whether your home has lead paint. They can also tell you
whether work is being done safely and according to the MA Lead Law and the Deleading &
Lead Safe Renovation Regulations.
Is my home's water safe?
The water provided to your home by Massachusetts Water Resource Authority (MWRA) is
safe. They test it regularly.
The service line that connects your home to the MWRA's water may contain lead. Find out
whether your home's service line is made from lead by checking the Boston Water and Sewer
Commission’s (BWSC) lead service line map at www.bwsc.org or by calling 617-989-7888.

question: My landlord is deducting my security deposit for things that were broken when I moved in. What can I do? (MA)
response:
In Massachusetts, your landlord cannot deduct from your security deposit for damages that were already present when you moved in. Here are steps you can take:

1. **Statement of Condition**: If you have a Statement of Condition that documents the pre-existing damages when you moved in, present it to your landlord. This document can serve as evidence that the damages were not caused by you.

2. **Demand Letter**: You can send a demand letter to your landlord requesting the return of your security deposit. Make sure to include evidence such as the Statement of Condition or any photos you took when you moved in. Send the letter by certified mail, return receipt requested, and keep a copy for your records. [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 3: Security Deposits (https://www.masslegalhelp.org/sites/default/files/2025-10/03%20Security%20Deposits%202025-%20Updated%208-13-25.pdf)]

3. **Legal Action**: If your landlord does not respond to your demand letter or refuses to return your deposit, you can take them to court. You may be entitled to up to three times the amount of your deposit, plus interest and court fees. [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 3: Security Deposits (https://www.masslegalhelp.org/sites/default/files/2025-10/03%20Security%20Deposits%202025-%20Updated%208-13-25.pdf)]

For further assistance, consider consulting an attorney or reaching out to legal aid resources such as MassLegalHelp.org or Greater Boston Legal Services.

question: How do I file a complaint about housing code violations in Boston?
response:
To file a complaint about housing code violations in Boston, you should contact the local health authority responsible for enforcing the state housing code, 105 CMR 410. In Boston, this is typically the Inspectional Services Department. They are responsible for conducting inspections, issuing orders to correct violations, and ensuring compliance with the housing code.

For more information, you can visit the Massachusetts government website on landlord and tenant law: [Massachusetts law about landlord and tenant | Mass.gov](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/massachusetts-law-about-landlord-and-tenant).

If you need further assistance, consider reaching out to legal aid resources such as MassLegalHelp.org or Greater Boston Legal Services.

In Massachusetts city and town local health authorities (LHA) enforce the state housing code, 105 CMR 410. question: Is my landlord required to provide heat in Massachusetts? What temperature?
response:
Yes, your landlord is required to provide heat in Massachusetts. According to the Massachusetts State Sanitary Code, landlords must provide and maintain a heating system capable of heating every habitable room and every room containing a toilet, shower, or bathtub. The heating system must be able to maintain a temperature of at least 68°F (20°C) during the day (7 AM to 11 PM) and at least 64°F (17°C) at night (11 PM to 7 AM) from September 15 to May 31. The temperature should not exceed 78°F (25°C) at any time.

question: Can I sue my landlord in small claims court for not returning my security deposit in MA?
response:
Yes, you can sue your landlord in small claims court in Massachusetts if they fail to return your security deposit. question: My landlord stopped paying the electric bill, and I'm worried about losing service. What can I do according to Massachusetts law?
response:
In Massachusetts, if your landlord is responsible for paying the electric bill and fails to do so, resulting in a potential shut-off, this may constitute a breach of the State Sanitary Code and your right to quiet enjoyment. You have several options:

1. **Legal Action**: You can take legal action against your landlord for failing to provide utilities. This can include suing for money damages or seeking a court order to compel the landlord to restore services. If successful, you may be entitled to up to three months' rent in damages and attorney's fees. [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 13: When to Take Your Landlord to Court (https://www.masslegalhelp.org/sites/default/files/2025-03/13%20Taking%20Landlords%20to%20Court%202025.pdf)]

2. **Consumer Protection**: If your landlord's actions are considered unfair or deceptive, such as intentionally shutting off your heat or electricity, you may have a claim under the Massachusetts Consumer Protection Act (Chapter 93A). This could entitle you to damages, including double or triple damages if the landlord's actions were willful. [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 13: When to Take Your Landlord to Court (https://www.masslegalhelp.org/sites/default/files/2025-03/13%20Taking%20Landlords%20to%20Court%202025.pdf)]

3. **Special Protections Against Shut-offs**: If you or someone in your household is seriously ill and you cannot afford to pay the bills due to financial hardship, utility companies cannot shut off your service. You would need a medical professional to certify the illness to the utility company. [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 6: Utilities (https://www.masslegalhelp.org/sites/default/files/2025-02/06%20Utilities%202025_0.pdf)]

For specific guidance and assistance, consider contacting a local legal aid organization such as Greater Boston Legal Services or visiting MassLegalHelp.org. Consulting with an attorney can also provide you with tailored advice for your situation.

2. Breach of Quiet Enjoyment or Interference
with Utilities
In Massachusetts, if a landlord interferes with your utilities or fails to make
repairs which result in your inability to use and enjoy your apartment, this may
be a breach of quiet enjoyment. The fact that you might owe rent does not
prevent you from bringing this type of lawsuit.
You may sue your landlord for money damages or court orders in the following
situations:
 If your landlord is required to furnish utilities or other services and they
intentionally fail to provide them. Common situations include failure to
provide hot water or heat, or failure to fix the furnace or boiler.
 If your landlord is required to provide utilities or other services and they
directly or indirectly interfere with the furnishing of them. That might also

include a landlord’s failure to pay utility bills that are their responsibility,
and the failure to pay results in the utility being shut off.
 If your landlord transfers the responsibility for payment for the utility to
you without your consent.
 If your landlord attempts to lock you out of your home.
 If your landlord moves you out of your apartment without first taking you
to court.
 If your landlord entered your home without your permission or notice.
 If the landlord in any other way intentionally interferes with your "quiet
enjoyment" of your apartment.15
Some examples that violate your right to the quiet enjoyment of your apartment
are:
 Repeated flooding of your apartment because of a plumbing problem that
the landlord knows about but is not adequately repaired.16
 The landlord's failure to provide adequate heat during the heating season
even if they could not afford to buy heating oil.17
 The landlord’s failure or refusal to fix the furnace or boiler, even when the
tenant is responsible for paying the fuel.
 The landlord converts your private space into a common space, like a
porch or basement that used to be accessible only to you.18
 Excessive noise from other tenants under the landlord's control.19
 A ringing fire alarm that continues for a 24-hour period because the
landlord failed to stop the ringing.20
a. What are the remedies if my landlord interfered with utilities
or breach of quiet enjoyment?
If you can prove that a landlord violated your quiet enjoyment, you may be
entitled to money damages. The money damages the court awards you will be
equal to either 3 months' rent or your actual loss, whichever is greater (minus any
rent you may owe). Your actual loss might include the money you had to pay to
eat in a restaurant while you were unable to get into your apartment, damage to
your property from a leaky roof, or the difference in value between your
apartment with a weathertight roof and your apartment with a leaky roof (in other
words, your breach of warranty damages).21

Special Protections Against Shut-offs
Customers are often protected against a utility company's shutting off their
service, even if they cannot afford to pay their bills. These special protections are
discussed below.
1. Serious Illness or Personal Safety
a. Electric, Gas, and Water
Electric, gas, and private water companies21 cannot shut off your service if you,
your child, or someone else in your household is seriously ill and you cannot
afford to pay your bills because of financial hardship.22 The utility companies
must treat any medical condition that a doctor, nurse practitioner or physician’s
assistant considers a serious illness as a serious illness, unless the company seeks
a hearing at the DPU to challenge the medical letter. Serious illness can include
mental health conditions such as major depression, anxiety disorder, Post-
Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD), and Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder
(ADHD). It can also include chronic physical health problems such as diabetes,
asthma, and fibromyalgia. Or, it can be a temporary serious illness such as
pneumonia or the flu.
To protect yourself against a shut-off, you should take the following steps as
soon as possible:
§ Contact your doctor, physician’s assistant, nurse practitioner, or the local
Board of Health and explain your situation. Ask them to immediately
contact the utility company by phone and tell the company that you are or
someone in your household is seriously ill. Make sure the doctor or Board
of Health has your name and address to give to the utility.
Within seven days of this initial phone contact, the medical professional or
Board of Health must send a letter to the utility company certifying the
illness. See the sample letter (Form 7) and sample form letter (Form 8)
that can be given to your doctor to fill out. Tell your doctor to include the
words "serious illness" in the letter and to describe the illness. If it is a
chronic or long-term illness, the doctor should include the words "chronic
illness" in the letter. A letter that states that the illness is a "chronic illness"
will result in 180 days of protection before you have to renew, while a
letter that does not state this will result in only 90 days of protection. If
you are uncomfortable having the utility know the type of illness, a letter
from the medical practitioner that simply includes the words “serious
illness” or “chronic, serious illness” should be sufficient.

4. Violation of Consumer Protection Law
The Massachusetts legislature has recognized that tenants are consumers of one
of the most significant consumer products—housing.29 Under the state Consumer
Protection Act, called “Chapter 93A,” it is illegal for a landlord to threaten,
attempt, or actually use any unfair or deceptive acts against you or anyone in
your house.30 For example, if your landlord intentionally shuts off your heat, this
would be an unfair or deceptive act that violates the Consumer Protection Act.
If your landlord acts in an unfair or deceptive way and this causes you to be
"injured,"31 you can take them to court, and possibly get money damages or an
injunction against them. An injury can include not only actual out of pocket loss,
but other types of harm, such as emotional distress,32 and even loss of time at
work. You may also be entitled to reasonable attorney's fees and the amount of
your actual loss.33 If you can show that your landlord should have known their
acts were unfair or deceptive, you can sometimes get double or triple the amount
of your money damages.34
Not all landlords, however, are covered by the Consumer Protection Act. If you
live in a 2- or 3-family building and the landlord lives in the building with you,
the Consumer Protection Act may not apply.35 If you live in a 2- or 3-family
building and the landlord lives in the building and uses the rent money to pay the
bills, then the Consumer Protection Act does not apply.36 Public housing tenants
cannot recover damages under the Consumer Protection Act for a housing
authority's breach of the warranty of habitability.37 If, however, you live in any
other situation, you can use this law to enforce your rights.

An unfair or deceptive act can be any action that violates existing laws or
regulations that protect your health, safety, or welfare.38 This can include:
 Violations of the local building codes, housing codes, and state Sanitary
Code;
 Violations of the Attorney General’s consumer protection regulations;39
 Retaliation;
 Charging you for utilities without a written agreement.
 Unfair debt collection practices;
 Refusing to make repairs after the landlord has notice;
 Violating your right to quiet enjoyment;
 Breaching the warranty of habitability;

question: I'm renting an apartment in Boston and my lease is for 12 months. What are my rights regarding the security deposit my landlord is holding?
response:
In Massachusetts, if your landlord is holding a security deposit, they must adhere to specific legal requirements:

1. **Amount**: The security deposit cannot exceed one month's rent. [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 3: Security Deposits]

2. **Receipt and Bank Account**: Your landlord must provide you with a receipt within 30 days of receiving your security deposit. This receipt must include the bank and account information where your deposit is held, as it must be kept in a separate bank account in Massachusetts. [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 3: Security Deposits]

3. **Interest**: Your landlord is required to pay you interest on your security deposit annually. If they fail to do so, you can deduct the interest from your rent. [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 3: Security Deposits]

4. **Use of Deposit**: The security deposit can only be used for unpaid rent or to repair damages caused by you or your guests, beyond normal wear and tear. It cannot be used for routine cleaning or small repairs. [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 3: Security Deposits]

5. **Return of Deposit**: Your landlord must return your security deposit, with interest, within 30 days after you move out, provided there are no damages or unpaid rent. If they fail to do so, you can send a demand letter and potentially sue for up to three times the deposit amount in small claims court. [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 3: Security Deposits]

6. **Statement of Condition**: If your landlord takes a security deposit, they must provide a Statement of Condition within 10 days of your move-in. If they do not, you can create your own and send it to them. [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 3: Security Deposits]

For more detailed information or if you encounter issues, you may want to consult resources like MassLegalHelp.org or contact Greater Boston Legal Services.

question: I just found out my landlord is selling the building. What happens to my security deposit?
response:
When your landlord sells the building, your security deposit should be transferred to the new owner. The new landlord has 45 days to send you a notice about your security deposit, last month's rent, and any interest owed. If the new landlord does not send you this notice by the deadline, the old landlord must return your deposit, plus interest. If 45 days pass and you have not heard from the new landlord, you should write to the old landlord to demand that they return your money, plus interest. If the old landlord does not return your money, you can sue them for three times the amount they owe you. 

Additionally, you should not be required to pay another security deposit or last month's rent to the new owner. The new owner is responsible for your security deposit, last month's rent, and interest, even if they never received it from the old landlord. 

For more information, you can refer to the Massachusetts security deposit law [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 3: Security Deposits (https://www.masslegalhelp.org/sites/default/files/2025-10/03%20Security%20Deposits%202025-%20Updated%208-13-25.pdf)].

question: Can my landlord in Boston legally require me to pay for the cost of repairing normal wear and tear when I move out?
response:
No, your landlord in Boston cannot legally require you to pay for the cost of repairing normal wear and tear when you move out. According to Massachusetts law, a lease must not include terms that require the tenant to pay for the cost of repairing ordinary wear and tear to the apartment. Additionally, landlords cannot use a security deposit to cover costs for reasonable wear and tear, such as routine painting and cleaning, new locks and keys, and small carpentry repairs. [Source: Attorney General's Guide to Landlord and Tenant Rights (https://www.mass.gov/guides/the-attorney-generals-guide-to-landlord-and-tenant-rights); Legal Tactics Ch. 3: Security Deposits (https://www.masslegalhelp.org/sites/default/files/2025-10/03%20Security%20Deposits%202025-%20Updated%208-13-25.pdf)].

## Key rules for security deposits

### What landlords can collect at start of tenancy
A landlord may only ask a tenant for: first month's rent, last month's rent, a security deposit (max one month's rent), and cost of a new lock and key.

### Holding requirements
- Must be deposited in a Massachusetts bank in an interest-bearing account
- Must be kept separate from landlord's money
- Landlord must provide tenant with bank name, address, and account number within 30 days
- Failure to comply entitles tenant to immediate return of deposit

### Statement of condition
- Must be provided within 10 days of tenancy start or receipt of deposit
- Must list all existing damage
- Tenant has 15 days to add or modify the statement

### Interest on security deposit
- Landlord must pay 5% annual interest or the actual bank interest (whichever is less)
- Interest must be paid annually or tenant may deduct from rent
- If not paid within 30 days of year end, tenant may deduct from next rent payment

### Return of security deposit
- Must be returned within 30 days after tenancy ends
- Landlord may deduct: unpaid rent, unpaid water charges, tax escalation amounts, reasonable repair costs for tenant-caused damage (not normal wear and tear)
- If deducting for damages: must provide itemized list sworn under penalty of perjury with repair estimates/receipts

### Triple damages
- Tenant entitled to 3x the deposit amount plus interest, court costs, and attorney's fees if landlord:
  - Fails to deposit in proper bank account
  - Fails to transfer deposit to successor
  - Fails to return deposit within 30 days

question: Can my landlord in Boston legally turn off my heat during the winter if I'm late on rent?
response:
No, your landlord cannot legally turn off your heat during the winter, even if you are late on rent. In Massachusetts, landlords are required to provide heat from September 15 through May 31. If the heat goes off, you should contact your landlord immediately. If they do not fix the problem, you can call the local Board of Health to report the issue. The law requires the Board of Health to inspect your apartment within 24 hours. Additionally, if your landlord turns off your heat, you can ask a court to order the landlord to turn it back on. [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 6: Utilities (https://www.masslegalhelp.org/sites/default/files/2025-02/06%20Utilities%202025_0.pdf)].

If you need further assistance, consider reaching out to legal aid resources like MassLegalHelp.org or Greater Boston Legal Services.

f. Bad Conditions
Under Massachusetts law, all landlords owe tenants what is called a warranty of
habitability. This means that your landlord must provide you with a safe and
habitable living environment that is free from any violations of the State Sanitary
Code. If your landlord does not keep your apartment in good condition, for example

Bad conditions as a defense
When your landlord knows about conditions that violate the state Sanitary Code
prior to you falling behind on your rent and allows these conditions to remain
uncorrected, you may have a defense that can prevent your eviction in a non-
payment or no-fault eviction case.169 This defense can be used by:
1. Tenants who are being evicted for non-payment of rent.
2. Tenants who are being evicted for a reason that is not the tenant's fault,
often referred to as a no-fault eviction. A no-fault eviction would be, for
example, if you refuse to pay a rent increase or if your landlord wants the
apartment for a family member.
3. All "occupants" of residential property, except people who have been
living in a hotel, motel, or lodging or rooming house for less than 3
consecutive months.170
If you are being evicted for a reason that the landlord claims is your fault, such
as disturbing other tenants or destroying property, you may not be able to use
bad conditions as a defense to prevent an eviction. In this situation, if your
landlord wants to prevent you from raising bad conditions as a defense, they must
send you a Notice to Quit that specifies the reasons for the eviction.171 A judge may
still allow you to bring up conditions-based claims against your landlord (to offset
any money damages your landlord claims against you), but your claims would not
provide a defense to the eviction case.172
If your defense is based on bad conditions, a judge must be convinced of the
following things:
 Bad conditions existed.
 Your landlord knew about the bad conditions before you were behind in
your rent.
 Neither you nor anyone else under your control caused the bad conditions.
 You do not live in a hotel or a motel or hotel or you have lived in a
rooming house for more than 3 months.
 The conditions can be repaired without you moving out.173
1. Bad conditions existed. The best way to prove that the bad conditions
exist or existed, and that the landlord has violated the state Sanitary Code,
is with a certified inspection report from the Board of Health.174 A

Common Problems and Situations to
Avoid
1. Another Person's Bill
a. Deserted spouse and domestic violence situations
A victim of domestic violence who remains in the home after the perpetrator
leaves (whether after getting an order that the perpetrator leave, or for other
reasons) is not responsible for bills rendered in the name of the perpetrator. To
obtain the benefit of this rule, you should call the utility company and ask that a
new account be opened in your name. You should do this as quickly as possible.
If you do not inform the company that your spouse or domestic partner has left, a
dispute will often arise as to when they actually left. The company may also
claim that you accepted responsibility for your spouse's old bills by leaving the
account in their name for as long as you did. Therefore, it is strongly
recommended that you make the change promptly.
b. Roommate
When a roommate who is the customer named on the utility bill moves out of
an apartment, the remaining roommate is not responsible for the departed
roommate's bills.39 For purposes of this rule, two unmarried people living
together would be considered “ roommates.”
c. Landlord Transfers Bill to Tenant
When a landlord wishes to transfer responsibility for a utility bill from themself
to a tenant, they cannot simply do so by calling the company. The tenant must
agree in writing with the landlord and the utility must be separately metered.40 If
you have not agreed in writing to a utility bill being put in your name, call the
utility company and ask that the bill be taken out of your name. If your landlord
then refuses to pay the bill, the company cannot shut off your service without
giving you notice. For more information, see the section in this chapter called
Your Right to Continued Service.

question: Can my landlord in Boston evict me because I reported a building code violation to the city?
response:
No, your landlord cannot legally evict you for reporting a building code violation to the city. Under Massachusetts law, it is illegal for a landlord to retaliate against a tenant for reporting violations of health or building codes. This protection is outlined in MGL c.186, s.18, which states that any reprisal against a tenant for such actions is prohibited and can result in the landlord being liable for damages. If you receive a notice of termination or rent increase within six months of reporting a violation, it creates a rebuttable presumption of retaliation, which the landlord must overcome with clear and convincing evidence. 

For more information, you can refer to the Massachusetts General Laws or seek assistance from legal aid resources such as MassLegalHelp.org or Greater Boston Legal Services. 

[Source: MGL c.186 s.18 - Anti-Retaliation Protection for Tenants (https://malegislature.gov/Laws/GeneralLaws/PartII/TitleI/Chapter186/Section18)]

f. Bad Conditions
Under Massachusetts law, all landlords owe tenants what is called a warranty of
habitability. This means that your landlord must provide you with a safe and
habitable living environment that is free from any violations of the State Sanitary
Code. If your landlord does not keep your apartment in good condition, for example
if your apartment has inadequate heat or rodent infestation, they have broken or
“breached” the Warranty of Habitability.168
380 ▲ Chapter 12: Evictions

Bad conditions as a defense
When your landlord knows about conditions that violate the state Sanitary Code
prior to you falling behind on your rent and allows these conditions to remain
uncorrected, you may have a defense that can prevent your eviction in a non-
payment or no-fault eviction case.169 This defense can be used by:
1. Tenants who are being evicted for non-payment of rent.
2. Tenants who are being evicted for a reason that is not the tenant's fault,
often referred to as a no-fault eviction. A no-fault eviction would be, for
example, if you refuse to pay a rent increase or if your landlord wants the
apartment for a family member.
3. All "occupants" of residential property, except people who have been
living in a hotel, motel, or lodging or rooming house for less than 3
consecutive months.170
If you are being evicted for a reason that the landlord claims is your fault, such
as disturbing other tenants or destroying property, you may not be able to use
bad conditions as a defense to prevent an eviction. In this situation, if your
landlord wants to prevent you from raising bad conditions as a defense, they must
send you a Notice to Quit that specifies the reasons for the eviction.171 A judge may
still allow you to bring up conditions-based claims against your landlord (to offset
any money damages your landlord claims against you), but your claims would not
provide a defense to the eviction case.172
If your defense is based on bad conditions, a judge must be convinced of the
following things:
 Bad conditions existed.
 Your landlord knew about the bad conditions before you were behind in
your rent.
 Neither you nor anyone else under your control caused the bad conditions.
 You do not live in a hotel or a motel or hotel or you have lived in a
rooming house for more than 3 months.
 The conditions can be repaired without you moving out.173
1. Bad conditions existed. The best way to prove that the bad conditions
exist or existed, and that the landlord has violated the state Sanitary Code,
is with a certified inspection report from the Board of Health.174 A
certified inspection report is one signed under the pains and penalties of
perjury.175

[MGL c.186 s.18 - Anti-Retaliation Protection for Tenants (https://malegislature.gov/Laws/GeneralLaws/PartII/TitleI/Chapter186/Section18)]
Section 18: Reprisal for reporting violations of law or for tenant's union activity; damages and costs; notice of termination, presumption; waiver in leases or other rental agreements prohibited

Any person or agent thereof who threatens to or takes reprisals against any tenant of residential premises for the tenant's act of:
- commencing, proceeding with, or obtaining relief in any judicial or administrative action the purpose of which action is to obtain damages under, or otherwise enforce, any federal, state or local law, regulation, by-law or ordinance, which has as its objective the regulation of residential premises; or
- exercising the tenant's rights pursuant to section one hundred and twenty-four D of chapter one hundred and sixty-four; or
- reporting to the board of health or, in the city of Boston to the commissioner of housing inspection or to any other board having as its objective the regulation of residential premises a violation or a suspected violation of any health or building code or of any other municipal by-law or ordinance, or state or federal law or regulation which has as its objective the regulation of residential premises; or
- reporting or complaining of such violation or suspected violation in writing to the landlord or to the agent of the landlord; or
- for organizing or joining a tenants' union or similar organization

shall be liable for damages which shall not be less than one month's rent or more than three month's rent, or the actual damages sustained by the tenant, whichever is greater, and the costs of the suit, including a reasonable attorney's fee.

The receipt of any notice of termination of tenancy, except for nonpayment of rent, or, of increase in rent, or, of any substantial alteration in the terms of tenancy within six months after the tenant has commenced, proceeded with, or obtained relief in such action, exercised such rights, made such report or complaint, or organized or joined such tenants' union or within six months after any other person has taken such action or actions on behalf of the tenant or in, or relating to, the building in which the tenant resides, shall create a rebuttable presumption that such notice or other action is a reprisal against the tenant for engaging in such activities.

Such presumption shall be rebutted only by clear and convincing evidence that such person's action was not a reprisal against the tenant and that such person had sufficient independent justification for taking such action, and would have in fact taken such action, in the same manner and at the same time the action was taken, regardless of tenants engaging in, or the belief that tenants had engaged in, activities protected under this section.

Any waiver of this provision in any lease or other rental agreement shall be void and unenforceable.

k. Violation of Consumer Protection Law
The Massachusetts legislature has recognized that tenants are consumers of one of
the most significant consumer products—housing.192 Under the state Consumer
Protection Act, it is illegal for a landlord to threaten, attempt, or actually use any
unfair or deceptive acts against you or anyone in your house.193
 If your landlord is covered by the Consumer Protection Act and is not a
housing authority, non-profit, or the owner-occupant of a 2- or 3-family
property,194 you may have a defense and counterclaim to a non-payment or
no-fault eviction.195
Chapter 12: Evictions ▲ 385

Consumer Protection Law as a Defense
 If you are facing eviction for non-payment or no-fault and you can prove
that the landlord acted in a way that was unfair or deceptive and that you
suffered injury or loss, the court should not allow the landlord to evict
you. Some examples of unfair or deceptive acts are outlined in the
Attorney General’s regulations that cover landlord-tenant relationships: 196
 The landlord charged you late fees before your rent was 30 days late.
 The landlord charged a rent amount that you never agreed to.
 The landlord charged you with a constable or court fee unlawfully.
 There are unlawful terms in your lease.197
 The landlord failed to fix conditions of disrepair in your home after you
gave them notice of the problems.198
 The landlord failed to maintain the apartment up to the minimum
standards in the health code.
 The landlord failed to comply with the security deposit statute.
Consumer Protection Law as a Counterclaim
 If there is a violation of the Consumer Protection Law, tenants are entitled
to actual damages suffered as a result of the landlord’s conduct as well as
attorney’s fees and costs. If the landlord’s conduct was willful and
knowing, a court may double and triple the damages.199
l. Personal Injury Claims and Lead Paint Poisoning
If you have been injured due to your landlord's negligence or your child has been
poisoned by lead paint, you can bring a counterclaim for your injuries. These legal
claims, however, can be complicated and may involve substantial amounts of
money. It is best to speak to a lawyer about bringing one of these claims. You may
be better off bringing the claim as a separate lawsuit against your landlord as
opposed to a counterclaim. If you bring these claims as counterclaims, you will not
be able to sue your landlord for these claims later. For example, if your child has
been exposed to lead, you may not know how badly they have been hurt until many
years after the exposure and so you would most likely not want to bring a claim at
the time of your eviction case.

question: What steps should I take to prepare for an eviction court hearing in Boston?
response:
To prepare for an eviction court hearing in Boston, you should follow these steps:

1. **Understand the Court Process**: Familiarize yourself with the eviction process, including the First Tier Court Event, which is a mandatory mediation session. If you do not settle the case during mediation, you will receive a date for a hearing or trial. [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 12: Evictions (https://www.masslegalhelp.org/sites/default/files/2025-03/12%20Evictions%202025.pdf)]

2. **Consider Transferring to Housing Court**: If your case is in district court, you may transfer it to housing court, where judges are more familiar with housing laws. To do this, fill out a Notice to Transfer form and file it with the district court, housing court, and your landlord or their attorney by the day before the original court date. [Source: Boston Housing Court (https://www.boston.gov/boston-housing-court)]

3. **Prepare Your Answer**: After receiving a notice of the First Tier Court event, fill out an answer document. This document should include your defenses and any counterclaims against your landlord. Defenses can help prevent eviction, and counterclaims can potentially reduce the rent you owe. [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 12: Evictions (https://www.masslegalhelp.org/sites/default/files/2025-03/12%20Evictions%202025.pdf)]

4. **Gather Evidence and Witnesses**: Prepare any evidence that supports your case, such as documents or photographs. Notify any witnesses of the time and place they should be in court. [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 12: Evictions (https://www.masslegalhelp.org/sites/default/files/2025-03/12%20Evictions%202025.pdf)]

5. **Prepare a Statement**: Write a brief statement summarizing how the landlord violated the law and why you should not be evicted. Use your answer form to help you with this. [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 12: Evictions (https://www.masslegalhelp.org/sites/default/files/2025-03/12%20Evictions%202025.pdf)]

6. **Plan for Court Day**: Be prepared to spend the entire day in court, as it is difficult to predict when your case will be called. Plan ahead for time off work or childcare. [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 12: Evictions (https://www.masslegalhelp.org/sites/default/files/2025-03/12%20Evictions%202025.pdf)]

7. **Answer When Your Name Is Called**: Make sure to be present and answer when your name is called in court to avoid being defaulted and losing your case. [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 12: Evictions (https://www.masslegalhelp.org/sites/default/files/2025-03/12%20Evictions%202025.pdf)]

For more detailed guidance, consider consulting legal aid resources such as MassLegalHelp.org or contacting Greater Boston Legal Services.

5. Transferring to Housing Court
As of 2017, every community in Massachusetts became covered by a housing court.
If your landlord files an eviction case in a district court, you have a right to transfer
your case to a housing court.87 The advantage of transferring an eviction case to
housing court is that judges in housing court are more familiar with housing laws
than district or superior court judges, who handle many different types of cases.
Housing courts also have the staff and expertise to better help people who do not
have a lawyer to complete the process.
There are 6 housing court divisions in Massachusetts and each division has satellite
sessions. For example, the Eastern Housing Court holds court in Boston, Chelsea,
and Somerville) 88 To figure out which housing court covers your area, see Chapter
14: Using the Court System.
To transfer your case, you only have to do two things:
1. Fill out a Transfer form (Booklet 5).
2. Deliver the form to the district court, the housing court, and your landlord
(or their lawyer) before your case is heard in the district court. Keep a
copy for yourself. You can deliver this form up until the day before the
trial date.
If you transfer your case to housing court, the housing court will send the landlord
notice of the First Court Event to serve on you. You should then have a new answer
date and mediation date.
6. Filing Your Answer
After you receive a notice of First Tier Court event, you must fill out a document
called an answer.89 The answer tells your side of the story and outlines what laws
protect you. An answer includes:
Defenses: The legal reasons why you should not be evicted. Defenses are
very important because they can help you win your case.
Counterclaims: Your legal claims for money against your landlord.
Counterclaims are important because you can use them to reduce the
amount of rent you owe your landlord, and sometimes they can help you
win your case. If your landlord owes you more money than you owe
them, you cannot be evicted in a non-payment or no-fault eviction
case. Also, in certain situations if you win a counterclaim and are able to
pay back the difference between what your landlord owes you and what
you owe your landlord, you can also win your eviction case.

separated from the defendants and plaintiffs. Even though it can be daunting,
remember that courts are there to serve the public and you have a right to have your
side of the story heard. Speak up for yourself and be sure to tell the judge what is
important to you about your case.
If you are representing yourself (pro se), you will need to pay very close attention to
what is happening. Read Chapter 14: Using the Court System for some practical
tips that will help you in court. Here are a few more things to keep in mind that
relate to eviction cases.
11. Preparing Your Case
Preparing to go to court is 90% of the battle. The other 10% is what happens the day
you go to court. The more prepared you are, the better off you will be. Use the
What to Bring to Court Checklist, which you will find in Booklet 1, and read
Preparing for Trial in Chapter 14: Using the Court System for more information
about preparing for trial. Plan to spend the day in court when your case is on for trial
because it is very difficult to know when your case will be called. Make sure to plan
ahead for time off of work or childcare.
Answer When Your Name Is Called
The first thing that will happen in court is that the clerk calls the names of
all the cases. When they call your name, say you are there. If you do not
answer, you will be defaulted and you will lose your case.
If Your Landlord Does Not Appear
If your landlord does not appear, the case should be dismissed. Ask the
clerk if you can file your appearance (a piece of paper that tells the court
that you appeared on the correct day). Then ask the clerk to give you a
copy of the order of dismissal.
Patience Is the Name of the Game
After the clerk calls the entire list of cases scheduled for the day, the trials
start. One of the most discouraging things about being in court is the
waiting. You may have to wait for hours before your case is called. You
may wind up going to court as many as three or four times, perhaps losing
pay each time you go.

question: Can I withhold rent if my apartment in Boston has serious code violations?
response:
Yes, you can withhold rent if your apartment in Boston has serious code violations. Under Massachusetts law, tenants have the right to withhold rent if the landlord fails to provide safe and habitable housing, as required by the warranty of habitability. Before withholding rent, you must ensure that:

1. Defective conditions exist in your apartment.
2. These conditions "endanger or materially impair" the health, safety, or well-being of anyone living in the home.
3. The landlord knows about the defective conditions before you were behind in your rent.
4. The conditions were not caused by you, a household member, guest, or someone under your control.
5. The landlord can make repairs without you having to permanently move out.

If you meet these requirements, you can legally withhold your rent. It is important to document the conditions and communicate with your landlord in writing. Additionally, it is advisable to place the withheld rent in a separate bank account to protect yourself if the landlord takes you to court. [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 8: Getting Repairs Made (https://www.masslegalhelp.org/sites/default/files/2025-03/08%20Getting%20Repairs%20Made%202025_0.pdf)].

For further guidance, consider consulting a tenant advocacy organization or a lawyer.

If your landlord does not make repairs after you have either notified them in
writing or they have been ordered by the Board of Health to make repairs, you

yourself of the options, you may want to consult with a tenant advocacy
organization or lawyer (see Directory).
1. Withhold Rent
One way to get your landlord to fix bad conditions is to withhold all or some of
your rent until the landlord actually makes the repairs. This is called "rent
withholding."46
Tenants have a right to withhold rent because landlords are obligated to provide
safe and habitable housing under the warranty of habitability. If a landlord
breaks this obligation, a tenant's obligation to pay the full amount of rent stops
until repairs are made.47 A tenant may want to withhold all or part of the rent,
depending on the seriousness of the violations.48 The law does not state how
much or for how long you can withhold.

right. Before you begin to withhold, read the next sections in this chapter very
carefully. Use the sample Rent Withholding Letter (Form 12).

the landlord and the tenant
Whether a tenancy is created by a lease or a tenancy-at-will, the tenant must pay rent, follow the rules agreed upon with the landlord, and accept responsibility for any damage to the apartment that is more than just "normal wear and tear". The landlord must provide an apartment that is safe, well-maintained, and in compliance with the Massachusetts Sanitary Code, and they must live up to any promises in the lease or rental agreement. The tenant has a right to occupy the apartment and the landlord may only enter under certain circumstances. The landlord must arrange with the tenant in advance to enter the apartment to make repairs, to inspect the condition of the apartment, or to show the apartment to prospective tenants, buyers or real estate agents. However, the landlord may enter an apartment without a tenant's approval if there is a mechanical/repair emergency that has the potential to damage the whole building, or if it appears that the tenant has abandoned the apartment.

## Terms of a rental agreement

Every rental agreement must have certain terms and is prohibited by law from containing certain other terms. The lease must set forth the name, address, and phone number of the owner, the person responsible for maintenance, and the person to whom the tenant can give copies of formal notices, complaints, or court papers.

The lease must not include illegal terms such as:
- Requiring the tenant to pay the cost of repairing ordinary wear and tear to the apartment
- Requiring the tenant to have the apartment professionally cleaned at the end of the lease
- Requiring the tenant to pay for repairs to parts of the building beyond the tenant's apartment
- Prohibiting the tenant from suing the landlord or reporting violations of the Sanitary Code
- Prohibiting the tenant from joining a tenants' union
- Requiring the tenant to pay a late fee if a rent payment is less than 30 days late

Yes, you may be able to withhold rent if your landlord has not fixed the heating in your apartment, as landlords are required to provide heat under the Massachusetts Sanitary Code. Before withholding rent, you must ensure that certain conditions are met:

1. Defective conditions must exist in your apartment.
2. These conditions must "endanger or materially impair" the health, safety, or well-being of anyone living in the home.

2. Breach of Quiet Enjoyment or Interference
with Utilities
In Massachusetts, if a landlord interferes with your utilities or fails to make
repairs which result in your inability to use and enjoy your apartment, this may
be a breach of quiet enjoyment. The fact that you might owe rent does not
prevent you from bringing this type of lawsuit.
You may sue your landlord for money damages or court orders in the following
situations:
 If your landlord is required to furnish utilities or other services and they
intentionally fail to provide them. Common situations include failure to
provide hot water or heat, or failure to fix the furnace or boiler.
 If your landlord is required to provide utilities or other services and they
directly or indirectly interfere with the furnishing of them. That might also
428 ▲ Chapter 13: When to Take Your Landlord to Court

include a landlord’s failure to pay utility bills that are their responsibility,
and the failure to pay results in the utility being shut off.
 If your landlord transfers the responsibility for payment for the utility to
you without your consent.
 If your landlord attempts to lock you out of your home.
 If your landlord moves you out of your apartment without first taking you
to court.
 If your landlord entered your home without your permission or notice.
 If the landlord in any other way intentionally interferes with your "quiet
enjoyment" of your apartment.15
Some examples that violate your right to the quiet enjoyment of your apartment
are:
 Repeated flooding of your apartment because of a plumbing problem that
the landlord knows about but is not adequately repaired.16
 The landlord's failure to provide adequate heat during the heating season
even if they could not afford to buy heating oil.17
 The landlord’s failure or refusal to fix the furnace or boiler, even when the
tenant is responsible for paying the fuel.
 The landlord converts your private space into a common space, like a
porch or basement that used to be accessible only to you.18
 Excessive noise from other tenants under the landlord's control.19
 A ringing fire alarm that continues for a 24-hour period because the
landlord failed to stop the ringing.20
a. What are the remedies if my landlord interfered with utilities
or breach of quiet enjoyment?
If you can prove that a landlord violated your quiet enjoyment, you may be
entitled to money damages. The money damages the court awards you will be
equal to either 3 months' rent or your actual loss, whichever is greater (minus any
rent you may owe). Your actual loss might include the money you had to pay to
eat in a restaurant while you were unable to get into your apartment, damage to
your property from a leaky roof, or the difference in value between your
apartment with a weathertight roof and your apartment with a leaky roof (in other
words, your breach of warranty damages).21

question: I just got an eviction notice in Boston. When do I need to appear in court, and what happens if I don't respond in time?
response:
When you receive an eviction notice in Boston, you will eventually receive a court notice with a date and time for your First Court Event, which is a mandatory mediation session. It is crucial to appear in court on the date and time specified in your court notice. If you fail to appear, the judge will likely rule in favor of the landlord, and the eviction will proceed. If the landlord fails to appear, the court may dismiss the case. [Source: What Happens During an Eviction (https://www.boston.gov/departments/housing/what-happens-during-eviction)].

If you do not respond to the eviction notice and do not appear in court, you will be defaulted, which means you automatically lose your case. This could result in an eviction order being issued against you. [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 12: Evictions (https://www.masslegalhelp.org/sites/default/files/2025-03/12%20Evictions%202025.pdf)].

For more detailed guidance and assistance, consider reaching out to legal aid resources such as MassLegalHelp.org or Greater Boston Legal Services.

5. Transferring to Housing Court
As of 2017, every community in Massachusetts became covered by a housing court.
If your landlord files an eviction case in a district court, you have a right to transfer
your case to a housing court.87 The advantage of transferring an eviction case to
housing court is that judges in housing court are more familiar with housing laws
than district or superior court judges, who handle many different types of cases.
Housing courts also have the staff and expertise to better help people who do not
have a lawyer to complete the process.
There are 6 housing court divisions in Massachusetts and each division has satellite
sessions. For example, the Eastern Housing Court holds court in Boston, Chelsea,
and Somerville) 88 To figure out which housing court covers your area, see Chapter
14: Using the Court System.
To transfer your case, you only have to do two things:
1. Fill out a Transfer form (Booklet 5).
2. Deliver the form to the district court, the housing court, and your landlord
(or their lawyer) before your case is heard in the district court. Keep a
copy for yourself. You can deliver this form up until the day before the
trial date.
If you transfer your case to housing court, the housing court will send the landlord
notice of the First Court Event to serve on you. You should then have a new answer
date and mediation date.
6. Filing Your Answer
After you receive a notice of First Tier Court event, you must fill out a document
called an answer.89 The answer tells your side of the story and outlines what laws
protect you. An answer includes:
Defenses: The legal reasons why you should not be evicted. Defenses are
very important because they can help you win your case.
Counterclaims: Your legal claims for money against your landlord.
Counterclaims are important because you can use them to reduce the
amount of rent you owe your landlord, and sometimes they can help you
win your case. If your landlord owes you more money than you owe
them, you cannot be evicted in a non-payment or no-fault eviction
case. Also, in certain situations if you win a counterclaim and are able to
pay back the difference between what your landlord owes you and what
you owe your landlord, you can also win your eviction case.

Why you should transfer

Boston Housing Court judges only hear housing cases. This is unlike District Court judges, who mostly hear criminal cases. In Boston Housing Court, the Clerk’s office staff knows the housing court process. Also, the Boston Housing Court offers mediation through trained specialists and legal help through the Lawyer for the Day Program.

How to transfer your case

You must complete a Notice to Transfer form and file it in three places:

* the District Court
* the Housing Court, and
* with your landlord (or your landlord’s attorney).

You must file the Notice to Transfer form by the day before the original court date. For example, if the trial date is on a Thursday, you must file and serve the Notice to Transfer on Wednesday. There is no cost to transfer a case to the Housing Court.

by Julia E. Devanthéry Italicized words are in the Glossary
The first and most important thing to know about eviction law in Massachusetts is
that a landlord cannot make a tenant move out of their home without going to court
first. No matter what a landlord or a landlord's lawyer says, a landlord must go
to court and obtain permission from a judge to evict a tenant.
If you get eviction papers and you want to stay in your apartment or you want more
time to find a new place, you must respond quickly to any documents you
receive and go to court to defend your case. Depending on your situation and
whether the landlord has followed the law, you may be able to prevent the eviction.
If you cannot prevent it, you still may be able to postpone it. In either case, if your
landlord has violated certain laws, you may be entitled to money to compensate you
for these violations.
If you do not defend yourself in an eviction case, chances are a judge will order you
to move out and you will have missed the opportunity to raise any legal claims or
negotiate an agreement about how to resolve the issues.
This chapter tells you how the eviction process works, what rights you have
throughout the process, how you can prevent an eviction, and how you might be
able to postpone an eviction while you find another place to live.
This chapter does not take the place of having a lawyer or provide you with every
detail involving evictions. But it will, along with forms at the end of the book, give
you enough information so that you can protect your rights.
When Can a Landlord Evict
In order to legally evict a tenant, a landlord must follow specific procedures. A
landlord must:
 Properly terminate a tenancy; and
 Get permission from a court to legally take possession of your apartment.
Evictions are not easy and can be expensive if a landlord fails to follow the law and
a tenant knows and enforces their rights.1 If you familiarize yourself with the steps
in the eviction process and are persistent, you may be able to stay in your apartment
longer or be awarded money for the landlord's violations of the law.

question: I'm struggling to pay my rent in a Boston public housing unit. Is there any way I can get an exemption or reduction due to my financial situation?
response:
For tenants in public housing, rent is typically calculated based on your income, so if your financial situation has changed, you may be eligible for a rent adjustment. It is important to report any changes in your income to the housing authority managing your unit. They can reassess your rent based on your current financial situation.

Additionally, Massachusetts offers programs to help with rent or other housing costs if you are facing eviction, foreclosure, or other emergencies. You can apply for assistance through programs like the Residential Assistance for Families in Transition (RAFT) and Emergency Rent and Mortgage Assistance (ERMA). More information about these programs can be found on the state's website [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 5: Rent (https://www.masslegalhelp.org/sites/default/files/2025-02/05%20Rent%202025%20v2.pdf)].

If you need further assistance, consider reaching out to local resources such as MassLegalHelp.org or Greater Boston Legal Services for guidance.

2. Keep Rent Receipts
It is important to keep a good record of your rent payments. If there is ever a
problem and your landlord claims that you did not pay, you will need proof that
you paid. Here is how to keep good records:
▪ Never give your landlord cash for rent unless you can get a receipt.
▪ Get receipts for all rent payments. The receipt should state the month and
year for which rent was paid.
▪ Ask the landlord for a receipt or make your own receipt for your landlord
to sign. Use this sample Rent Receipt (Form 2).
▪ Pay your rent with a check or money order and write on the front of the
check or money order the month and year for which rent is paid. Make a
copy of the check or money order, including any receipt stub.
▪ Keep proof of all rent payments in a safe place. Save all rent receipts,
cancelled checks, and copies of money orders with their stubs in a special
folder or envelope. If you pay rent via an online portal, take screenshots of
your monthly payments and save those.
▪ For multiple tenants contributing to rent, each should have their own proof
of rent paid. The best way is for each tenant to pay their part of the rent
directly to the landlord and keep proof of their payment. If there is a
disagreement later about whether the landlord gave someone permission to
be a tenant, each tenant will want proof that they paid rent, and that the
landlord accepted their rent.
Paying Rent
1. What If the Rent Is Late
As a tenant, you are obligated to pay only the rent you and your landlord have
agreed upon. You must pay the rent in advance, on or before the date you and the
landlord agreed rent is due. Often the agreed rent date is the first of the month.
If you are late paying the rent, a landlord may try to charge you a late fee or
penalty. It is against the law for landlords to charge late fees in some cases. See
below in Late Fees.9
A landlord may also try to evict you for repeated late payments or for non-
payment of rent. Most landlords do not send eviction notices if once in a while
tenants are several days late with the rent. Even if a landlord sends an eviction
notice, you may be able to stop the eviction by paying the rent you owe. See
below in Stopping an Eviction for Non-Payment or Late Payment.”

In Massachusetts, including Boston, landlords of private unsubsidized housing can generally charge as much rent as they want, as there is no legal limit on rent amounts in the private market. During a market emergency, there might be additional regulations or temporary measures put in place by local or state authorities. However, based on the information available, there is no specific mention of restrictions on rent increases during a market emergency in the provided sources.

you can afford.7 There is currently no legal limit to the amount of rent a landlord
can charge in the private unsubsidized housing market in Massachusetts.8
In private subsidized housing, public housing, or in a mobile home park covered
by a local rent control law, the rent a landlord can charge is controlled, and there
are procedures for increasing the amount. For more about:
▪ Public Housing
See the booklet Rent in Public Housing at
www.MassLegalHelp.org/housing/tenants-rights-in-public-housing
▪ Subsidized Housing
See Housing Programs in Legal Tactics: Finding Public & Subsidized
Housing at www.MassLegalHelp.org/housing/finding-housing-booklets
▪ Mobile Homes
See Chapter 16: Mobile Homes.
▲ Chapter 5: Rent

2. Keep Rent Receipts
It is important to keep a good record of your rent payments. If there is ever a
problem and your landlord claims that you did not pay, you will need proof that
you paid. Here is how to keep good records:
▪ Never give your landlord cash for rent unless you can get a receipt.
▪ Get receipts for all rent payments. The receipt should state the month and
year for which rent was paid.
▪ Ask the landlord for a receipt or make your own receipt for your landlord
to sign. Use this sample Rent Receipt (Form 2).
▪ Pay your rent with a check or money order and write on the front of the
check or money order the month and year for which rent is paid. Make a
copy of the check or money order, including any receipt stub.
▪ Keep proof of all rent payments in a safe place. Save all rent receipts,
cancelled checks, and copies of money orders with their stubs in a special
folder or envelope. If you pay rent via an online portal, take screenshots of
your monthly payments and save those.
▪ For multiple tenants contributing to rent, each should have their own proof
of rent paid. The best way is for each tenant to pay their part of the rent
directly to the landlord and keep proof of their payment. If there is a
disagreement later about whether the landlord gave someone permission to
be a tenant, each tenant will want proof that they paid rent, and that the
landlord accepted their rent.
Paying Rent
1. What If the Rent Is Late
As a tenant, you are obligated to pay only the rent you and your landlord have
agreed upon. You must pay the rent in advance, on or before the date you and the
landlord agreed rent is due. Often the agreed rent date is the first of the month.
If you are late paying the rent, a landlord may try to charge you a late fee or
penalty. It is against the law for landlords to charge late fees in some cases. See
below in Late Fees.9
A landlord may also try to evict you for repeated late payments or for non-
payment of rent. Most landlords do not send eviction notices if once in a while
tenants are several days late with the rent. Even if a landlord sends an eviction
notice, you may be able to stop the eviction by paying the rent you owe. See
below in Stopping an Eviction for Non-Payment or Late Payment.”

question: Can my landlord enter my apartment without notice to make repairs?
response:
In Massachusetts, a landlord generally cannot enter your apartment without notice to make repairs. The landlord must provide at least 48 hours' notice before entering for repairs, unless it is an emergency situation that could potentially damage the whole building. In non-emergency situations, the landlord should arrange with you in advance to enter the apartment for repairs, inspections, or to show the apartment to prospective tenants or buyers. [Source: Legal Tactics Ch. 8: Getting Repairs Made (https://www.masslegalhelp.org/sites/default/files/2025-03/08%20Getting%20Repairs%20Made%202025_0.pdf); Attorney General's Guide to Landlord and Tenant Rights (https://www.mass.gov/guides/the-attorney-generals-guide-to-landlord-and-tenant-rights)].

If you have further questions or need specific legal advice, consider consulting an attorney or visiting resources like MassLegalHelp.org or Greater Boston Legal Services.

Landlord's Right to Enter Your Home
Many landlords think that they can let themselves into your apartment any time
they want. This is not true.
Your landlord must have your permission to enter. If you do not give your
landlord permission to enter, the landlord can enter if there are terms of your
lease or written tenancy agreement which are legal and give the landlord
permission to enter or your landlord has a court order.
Under the law19, a lease may allow the landlord to enter your apartment so that

§ To inspect it during the last 30 days of your tenancy to determine if there
are damages that would lead to a reduction in the return of your security

If you have a lease and it states other reasons that your landlord can enter your

always best to be cooperative in allowing access for making repairs.
Getting an Inspection
Tenants in Massachusetts have a right to have their home inspected by a local
housing inspector. Before you call a housing inspector, you should make sure
you have given your landlord a chance to make repairs. If, however, you have
given your landlord a chance to make repairs and they refuse or don't reply, a
housing inspector can be helpful. Housing inspectors examine properties to see

the landlord and the tenant
Whether a tenancy is created by a lease or a tenancy-at-will, the tenant must pay rent, follow the rules agreed upon with the landlord, and accept responsibility for any damage to the apartment that is more than just "normal wear and tear". The landlord must provide an apartment that is safe, well-maintained, and in compliance with the Massachusetts Sanitary Code, and they must live up to any promises in the lease or rental agreement. The tenant has a right to occupy the apartment and the landlord may only enter under certain circumstances. The landlord must arrange with the tenant in advance to enter the apartment to make repairs, to inspect the condition of the apartment, or to show the apartment to prospective tenants, buyers or real estate agents. However, the landlord may enter an apartment without a tenant's approval if there is a mechanical/repair emergency that has the potential to damage the whole building, or if it appears that the tenant has abandoned the apartment.

## Terms of a rental agreement

Every rental agreement must have certain terms and is prohibited by law from containing certain other terms. The lease must set forth the name, address, and phone number of the owner, the person responsible for maintenance, and the person to whom the tenant can give copies of formal notices, complaints, or court papers.

The lease must not include illegal terms such as:
- Requiring the tenant to pay the cost of repairing ordinary wear and tear to the apartment
- Requiring the tenant to have the apartment professionally cleaned at the end of the lease
- Requiring the tenant to pay for repairs to parts of the building beyond the tenant's apartment
- Prohibiting the tenant from suing the landlord or reporting violations of the Sanitary Code
- Prohibiting the tenant from joining a tenants' union
- Requiring the tenant to pay a late fee if a rent payment is less than 30 days late

Retaliatory evictions are illegal.30 An example of a retaliatory eviction would
be if a rooming house owner attempts to evict you because you have

more information, see Chapter 12: Evictions - Retaliatory Evictions.

If your landlord refuses to make repairs after you notify them in writing
about conditions that violate the state Sanitary Code, you have the right to
make repairs and deduct the cost of repairs from your rent. If you have lived
in your rooming house for less than 3 months, this may involve complex

You have the same right to privacy as other tenants. A landlord is not
allowed to just enter your apartment. But you should allow a landlord access

to enter the apartment to make repairs. A landlord must provide at least 48

question: My apartment in Boston has been unbearably hot this winter, constantly over 78°F. Is my landlord violating any regulations?
response:
The Massachusetts Sanitary Code requires that landlords provide adequate heat during the heating season, which runs from September 15 to June 15. However, the code specifies minimum temperatures that must be maintained, not maximum temperatures. The minimum temperature requirement is 68°F during the day and 64°F at night. There is no specific regulation in the Massachusetts Sanitary Code that addresses maximum temperatures in winter.

If the excessive heat is causing discomfort or other issues, you may want to discuss the situation with your landlord to see if adjustments can be made. If the problem persists and affects your ability to enjoy your apartment, you might consider contacting your local Board of Health for further guidance.

For more detailed assistance, you may want to consult legal aid resources such as MassLegalHelp.org or Greater Boston Legal Services.

2. Breach of Quiet Enjoyment or Interference
with Utilities
In Massachusetts, if a landlord interferes with your utilities or fails to make
repairs which result in your inability to use and enjoy your apartment, this may
be a breach of quiet enjoyment. The fact that you might owe rent does not
prevent you from bringing this type of lawsuit.
You may sue your landlord for money damages or court orders in the following
situations:
 If your landlord is required to furnish utilities or other services and they
intentionally fail to provide them. Common situations include failure to
provide hot water or heat, or failure to fix the furnace or boiler.
 If your landlord is required to provide utilities or other services and they
directly or indirectly interfere with the furnishing of them. That might also

include a landlord’s failure to pay utility bills that are their responsibility,
and the failure to pay results in the utility being shut off.
 If your landlord transfers the responsibility for payment for the utility to
you without your consent.
 If your landlord attempts to lock you out of your home.
 If your landlord moves you out of your apartment without first taking you
to court.
 If your landlord entered your home without your permission or notice.
 If the landlord in any other way intentionally interferes with your "quiet
enjoyment" of your apartment.15
Some examples that violate your right to the quiet enjoyment of your apartment
are:
 Repeated flooding of your apartment because of a plumbing problem that
the landlord knows about but is not adequately repaired.16
 The landlord's failure to provide adequate heat during the heating season
even if they could not afford to buy heating oil.17
 The landlord’s failure or refusal to fix the furnace or boiler, even when the
tenant is responsible for paying the fuel.
 The landlord converts your private space into a common space, like a
porch or basement that used to be accessible only to you.18
 Excessive noise from other tenants under the landlord's control.19
 A ringing fire alarm that continues for a 24-hour period because the
landlord failed to stop the ringing.20
a. What are the remedies if my landlord interfered with utilities
or breach of quiet enjoyment?
If you can prove that a landlord violated your quiet enjoyment, you may be
entitled to money damages. The money damages the court awards you will be
equal to either 3 months' rent or your actual loss, whichever is greater (minus any
rent you may owe). Your actual loss might include the money you had to pay to
eat in a restaurant while you were unable to get into your apartment, damage to
your property from a leaky roof, or the difference in value between your
apartment with a weathertight roof and your apartment with a leaky roof (in other
words, your breach of warranty damages).21

f. Bad Conditions
Under Massachusetts law, all landlords owe tenants what is called a warranty of
habitability. This means that your landlord must provide you with a safe and
habitable living environment that is free from any violations of the State Sanitary
Code. If your landlord does not keep your apartment in good condition, for example
if your apartment has inadequate heat or rodent infestation, they have broken or
“breached” the Warranty of Habitability.168
380 ▲ Chapter 12: Evictions

Bad conditions as a defense
When your landlord knows about conditions that violate the state Sanitary Code
prior to you falling behind on your rent and allows these conditions to remain
uncorrected, you may have a defense that can prevent your eviction in a non-
payment or no-fault eviction case.169 This defense can be used by:
1. Tenants who are being evicted for non-payment of rent.
2. Tenants who are being evicted for a reason that is not the tenant's fault,
often referred to as a no-fault eviction. A no-fault eviction would be, for
example, if you refuse to pay a rent increase or if your landlord wants the
apartment for a family member.
3. All "occupants" of residential property, except people who have been
living in a hotel, motel, or lodging or rooming house for less than 3
consecutive months.170
If you are being evicted for a reason that the landlord claims is your fault, such
as disturbing other tenants or destroying property, you may not be able to use
bad conditions as a defense to prevent an eviction. In this situation, if your
landlord wants to prevent you from raising bad conditions as a defense, they must
send you a Notice to Quit that specifies the reasons for the eviction.171 A judge may
still allow you to bring up conditions-based claims against your landlord (to offset
any money damages your landlord claims against you), but your claims would not
provide a defense to the eviction case.172
If your defense is based on bad conditions, a judge must be convinced of the
following things:
 Bad conditions existed.
 Your landlord knew about the bad conditions before you were behind in
your rent.
 Neither you nor anyone else under your control caused the bad conditions.
 You do not live in a hotel or a motel or hotel or you have lived in a
rooming house for more than 3 months.
 The conditions can be repaired without you moving out.173
1. Bad conditions existed. The best way to prove that the bad conditions
exist or existed, and that the landlord has violated the state Sanitary Code,
is with a certified inspection report from the Board of Health.174 A
certified inspection report is one signed under the pains and penalties of
perjury.175

Common Problems and Situations to
Avoid
1. Another Person's Bill
a. Deserted spouse and domestic violence situations
A victim of domestic violence who remains in the home after the perpetrator
leaves (whether after getting an order that the perpetrator leave, or for other
reasons) is not responsible for bills rendered in the name of the perpetrator. To
obtain the benefit of this rule, you should call the utility company and ask that a
new account be opened in your name. You should do this as quickly as possible.
If you do not inform the company that your spouse or domestic partner has left, a
dispute will often arise as to when they actually left. The company may also
claim that you accepted responsibility for your spouse's old bills by leaving the
account in their name for as long as you did. Therefore, it is strongly
recommended that you make the change promptly.
b. Roommate
When a roommate who is the customer named on the utility bill moves out of
an apartment, the remaining roommate is not responsible for the departed
roommate's bills.39 For purposes of this rule, two unmarried people living
together would be considered “ roommates.”
c. Landlord Transfers Bill to Tenant
When a landlord wishes to transfer responsibility for a utility bill from themself
to a tenant, they cannot simply do so by calling the company. The tenant must
agree in writing with the landlord and the utility must be separately metered.40 If
you have not agreed in writing to a utility bill being put in your name, call the
utility company and ask that the bill be taken out of your name. If your landlord
then refuses to pay the bill, the company cannot shut off your service without
giving you notice. For more information, see the section in this chapter called
Your Right to Continued Service.

What is the Massachusetts Lead Law?
The Massachusetts Lead Law protects children from lead poisoning.
The Lead Law requires the removal or covering of any lead paint hazards in any home built
before 1978 where a child under the age of 6 lives. Lead paint hazards include loose lead
paint or lead paint on things like windows and door frames.
Homeowners and landlords are responsible for complying with the Lead Law. They are
required to make the home lead-safe if a child under 6 lives there.
Can a landlord refuse to rent to me or
evict me because of lead in the home?
No. According to MA laws and the Federal Fair Housing Act,
landlords CANNOT refuse to rent to you or evict you if you
have children or if the property has lead. Landlords are
responsible for correcting lead paint hazards in your home.
If you think a landlord has discriminated against you, call the
Boston Office of Fair Housing & Equity at 617-635-2500 or the
MA Commission Against Discrimination at 617-994-6000.
My landlord is doing work in my home. Is my family safe?
If you are unsure whether your landlord is doing work safely, call the Boston Childhood Lead
Poisoning Prevention Program (BCLPPP) at 617-534-5965.
BCLPPP inspectors can identify whether your home has lead paint. They can also tell you
whether work is being done safely and according to the MA Lead Law and the Deleading &
Lead Safe Renovation Regulations.

The water provided to your home by Massachusetts Water Resource Authority (MWRA) is
safe. They test it regularly.

question: Can my landlord in Boston be penalized if they don't fix a serious health code violation in my apartment after being ordered to?
response:
Yes, your landlord in Boston can be penalized if they fail to fix a serious health code violation after being ordered to do so. If a landlord does not comply with the state Sanitary Code, fines can range from $10 to $500 per day for violations. Additionally, if the landlord fails to provide essential services like heat or hot water, or interferes with your quiet enjoyment, they could face criminal penalties, including fines and potentially up to 6 months in jail. 

If a landlord fails to follow the terms of a court order, they may also be held in contempt and punished by the court. For example, a landlord who fails to make court-ordered repairs may be ordered to live in their building until the repairs are completed. 

For more information, you may want to consult an attorney or contact local legal aid resources such as MassLegalHelp.org or Greater Boston Legal Services.
